If you want to simply use apply_chat_template with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood: import torch from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModelForMultimodalLM model_id = "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(model_id). eval () messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "audio" , "url" : "https://huggingface.co/buckets/huggingface/audio-samples/resolve/bbaudio_question_39.mp3" , }, { "type" : "text" , "text" : "Answer the question." , }, ], } ] # Downloads the audio, decodes it as mono, resamples it to 24 kHz, pads it, creates input_values_mask, and expands the audio placeholders. inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , load_audio_backend= "auto" , ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) with torch.inference_mode(): output_ids = model.generate( **inputs, max_new_tokens= 128 , do_sample= False , ) # Decode only newly generated tokens prompt_length = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ] generated_text = processor.batch_decode( output_ids[:, prompt_length:], skip_special_tokens= True , ) print (generated_text[ 0 ]) The processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings. Tool Calling Muse Spark Open can do text-only and multimodal tool calling. You can make the model call tools as follows. from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModelForMultimodalLM MODEL_ID = "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B" # Load model processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID) model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained( MODEL_ID, dtype= "auto" , device_map= "auto" ) tools = [ { "type" : "function" , "function" : { "name" : "weather.get" , "description" : "Get the current weather for a city." , "parameters" : { "type" : "object" , "properties" : { "city" : { "type" : "string" }, }, "required" : [ "city" ], }, }, } ] messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "image" , "image" : "https://huggingface.co/datasets/merve/vl-test-suite/resolve/main/SF.png" }, { "type" : "text" , "text" : "I'm going to the city in this picture. What clothes should I wear?" }, ], }, ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, tools=tools, tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , add_generation_prompt= True , reasoning_strength= "high" ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs) response = processor.parse_response( completion, prefix=inputs[ "input_ids" ][ 0 ], tools=tools, ) print (response) Muse Spark Open uses a channel-based chat template (Harmony, first introduced by gpt-oss). Note that you don’t have to know about the internals, but it’s useful to check the channels the model routes to, in case you get low quality outputs. In the input message below: <|begin_of_text|> <|start|>system<|message|> You are a helpful AI assistant. Knowledge cutoff: 2026-01-04. Current date: ... ... <|eot|> <|start|>user<|message|>... <|eot|> <|start|>assistant <|start|>assistant is intentionally left open, it’s the model that chooses recipient with to= . The model has different recipients, e.g. self asks the model to reason, to=self<|message|>the model reasons here<|eom|> # reasoning <|start|>assistant to=user<|message|>final answer<|eot|> # final answer self is for reasoning, commentary are comments before and between tool calls visible to the end user, user is the final response. Tool-call routing is parsed as follows (assuming you have passed tools to apply_chat_template : <|start|>assistant to=weather.get<|message|> <atem:function_calls> <atem:invoke name="weather.get"> <atem:parameter name="city">San Francisco</atem:parameter> </atem:invoke> </atem:function_calls> <|eot|> Llama.cpp Muse Spark 2-bit running on Llama Server Muse Spark Open is integrated in llama.cpp and comes in the prebuilt binaries. You can install this with following command: curl -LsSf https://llama.app/install.sh | sh You can start the server as follows with quant suffix attached to model ID: llama serve -hf ggml-org/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-GGUF:Q2_K The repository containing quants is here . Once the server has started, you can head to localhost:9931 to chat with the built-in WebUI. From the web UI you can add audio and images for inference and adjust the reasoning lever. Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. We tested quants on Mac M3 Ultra (512GB). An imatrix-calibrated 2-bit quant runs at 18 tokens/s, with plenty of room free for the KV cache (304 GB used by the model). You can also query the server as follows. Feel free to check out the API reference for multimodality, tool calls and more. ## Text-only inference curl http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."}, {"role": "user", "content": "Write a limerick about python exceptions"} ] }' ## Image-text inference curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Authorization: Bearer <your-key>" \ -d '{"model":"muse-spark-open","messages":[{"role":"user","content":[ {"type":"text","text":"What is in this image?"}, {"type":"image_url","image_url":{"url":"data:image/png;base64,..."}} ]}],"temperature":0}' ## Audio-text inference curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Authorization: Bearer <your-key>" \ -d '{"model":"muse-spark-open","messages":[{"role":"user","content":[ {"type":"text","text":"Transcribe this audio."}, {"type":"input_audio","input_audio":{"data":"data:audio/wav;base64,..."}} ]}],"temperature":0}' llama.cpp team ships different quantized versions. We have tested Q2_K, Q4_K_S and Q_8 on Apple Silicon chips. You can run each quant by adding the quant id as suffix, llama serve -hf ggml-org/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B:Q2_K . SGLang The Muse Spark Open integration for SGLang supports text, image, audio, and video inputs. The NVFP4 reference configuration runs across four GB300 GPUs. From the SGLang integration environment, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and start the server: export MODEL_ID=meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 export CKPT="$(hf download "$MODEL_ID")" SGLANG_FLASHINFER_NVFP4_PER_TOKEN_ACTIVATION=1 \ uv run sglang_meta serve \ --model-path "$CKPT" \ --served-model-name "$MODEL_ID" \ --quantization modelopt_fp4 \ --moe-runner-backend flashinfer_trtllm \ --tp-size 4 \ --ep-size 4 \ --port 30000 The checkpoint includes the chat template, which we pass explicitly. The launcher configures the Muse reasoning and tool-call parsers. Send a request through the OpenAI-compatible API: curl http://localhost:30000/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4", "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": "Explain how a mixture-of-experts model works." }], "max_tokens": 2048 }' The response separates the reasoning trace in reasoning_content from the final answer in content . vLLM The Muse Spark Open reference integration for vLLM supports text and image inputs with the NVFP4 checkpoint that require blackwell series GPUs. After installing the reference plugin and its dependencies, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and launch the server: export MODEL_ID=meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 export CKPT="$(hf download "$MODEL_ID")" VLLM_ALLOW_LONG_MAX_MODEL_LEN=1 \ VLLM_PLUGINS=musespark1x_models,ptq_nvfp4 \ vllm serve "$CKPT" \ --served-model-name "$MODEL_ID" \ --tokenizer-mode musespark1x \ --config-format auto \ --load-format internal_safetensor \ --tensor-parallel-size 4 \ --enable-expert-parallel \ --max-model-len 131072 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 \ --reasoning-parser musespark1x \ --tool-call-parser musespark1x \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --port 8000 This configuration sets a 128K-token serving context. The plugin supplies the model implementation, checkpoint loader, and reasoning and tool-call parsers. Send a request using the same Hub model ID: curl http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4", "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": "Explain how a mixture-of-experts model works." }], "max_tokens": 2048 }' MLX Muse Spark Open is available in oMLX and mlx-lm today. oQ quants optimized for oMLX are available in 3-bit and 4-bit , ready to use right away. We tested the oQ3e quant on an M3 Ultra (512 GB). The model takes about 344 GB, leaving room for the KV cache, and runs at about 225 tok/s prefill and 21 tok/s generation with a 1024-token prompt and 128 generated tokens. Once you download the model through the oMLX interface, you can chat with it in the built-in chat UI. From the chat UI you can add images and adjust the reasoning effort on the fly, from low to xhigh. The model’s reasoning shows up as a collapsible thinking block, separate from the final answer. Note that it's not possible to turn reasoning off, and the default (Auto) uses xhigh. Set it to “low” if you want to use fewer tokens on easier tasks. The language model is also available in this PR of the official mlx-lm repository. You can run it on the same high-quality oQ3e quant like this: mlx_lm.generate --model mlx-community/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-oQ3e \ --prompt "Explain convolutional networks like I am 5" \ --max-tokens 5000 This is a big model, even the 3-bit quantization requires more than 256 GB of RAM, as explained above. You can also run distributed inference across multiple computers, please refer to the documentation for details. Deploying Muse Spark Open with Inference Endpoints You can deploy Muse Spark Open on Inference Endpoints with a pre-validated SGLang recipe for the NVFP4 variant which runs on either 8 × NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 98 GB with 131072 context length, or with 8 x NVIDIA H200 141GB if you want 1048576 context length instead. To deploy, run one command with the Hugging Face CLI: hf endpoints catalog deploy --repo meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 --name muse-spark Or open endpoints.huggingface.co/new/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 and select Create Endpoint. The endpoint exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with both Chat Completions API at /v1/chat/completions and Responses API at /v1/responses . curl "https://<your-endpoint>.endpoints.huggingface.cloud/v1/chat/completions" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $HF_TOKEN " \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4", "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "https://huggingface.co/datasets/merve/vl-test-suite/resolve/main/pills.jpg"}}, {"type": "text", "text": "Do any of the components in this supplement interact?"} ] }], "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false} }' Any OpenAI-compatible client works with the same URL and your Hugging Face token as the API key. Fine-tuning with TRL You can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer . This section shows how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples . First, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP

items.content: Back to Articles Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale Published October 16, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 37 +31 ben burtenshaw burtenshaw Follow merve merve Follow Pedro Cuenca pcuenq Follow Beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the new US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens , and is released under the Apache 2.0 license. Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model. Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post shows you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it. TL;DR 501B-parameter MoEs LLM with 23B active per token. 52 layers, 256 experts per MoE layer, 8 routed per token. Text in, text out with context window of 1M tokens. Checkpoint formats: BF16 , FP8 , and NVFP4 Reasoning that can stay in context across turns ( preserve_thinking ), tool calling with a dedicated grammar. The model supports five reasoning values: "low", "medium" (default), "high", "xhigh", and "max". Response template in the tokenizer. Speculative decoding drafter model with DFlash2 Day-0 libraries: transformers, SGLang, vLLM. Full-parameter RL with Miles. Ships with a Rust-based custom harness. Apache 2.0. Build with Beam Reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub: You could make a demo that uses the Beam model on Spaces You could quantize it for your favorite hardware You could generate a synthetic dataset for your favorite problem You could build an RL environment with or for Beam You could benchmark Beam and share the results. You could surprise us! If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page . We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts. What is Beam? Beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one. Attention The decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones. Inside the attention block (both layer types) The two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding . Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1 . It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling. Attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection. Mixture of Experts The first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters. The router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5. Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips. If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below. Residual Stream The residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth. Beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k) . The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state. Every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap. Long Context Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate. Context If all 52 layers were global Beam 32K tokens 6.5 GiB 1.2 GiB 128K tokens 26 GiB 4.6 GiB Full context (1M) 208 GiB 36.08 GiB These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache. Benchmark Results Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team. Beam (BF16) Beam (FP8) Beam (NVFP4) Agentic Coding / Terminal DeepSWE v1.1 43.3% 43.0% 42.7% SWE Bench Pro v2-Hard 76.5% 78.4% 78.6% SWE Bench Pro v1 66.1% 65.9% 65.6% Terminal Bench v2.1 80.1% 78.9% 78.2% SWE Atlas Codebase QnA 31.8% 32.2% 31.4% SWEBench Multilingual 78.3% 78.1% 77.5% SWEBench Verified 81.6% 80.2% 80.7% Reasoning AIME 2026 97.7% 98.0% 97.5% HLE (no tools) 36.0% 36.0% 34.8% HLE (with tools) 51.1% 51.1% 51.1% SciCode 49.2% 48.3% 46.9% CriPT AA 16.3% 17.4% 15.4% GPQA Diamond 90.6% 90.3% 89.3% LiveCodeBench 88.3% 88.1% 87.4% Tool Calling / Search AutomationBench - public split only 39.3 38.2 39.8% MCP Atlas 80.8% 81.5% 80.5% Tau3 Banking 36.1% 36.8% 35.4% BrowseComp w/ context management 76.8% 76.7% 75.6% DeepSearchQA w/ context management 80.5% 79.6% 81.1% General Capabilities AA-LCR 78.2% 79.4% 78.7% LongBench v2 67.5% 67.6% 67.2% IFBench 79.6% 80.7% 79.2% AA Omniscience (index) - public split only 10.8 8.8 9.8 Hardware Requirements The most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell. A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Plan for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection. Inference Support Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM. Transformers Install the latest version of transformers. pip install -U "transformers>=5.20.1" The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline: from transformers import pipeline pipe = pipeline( "text-generation" , model= "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B" , device_map= "auto" ) messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "Write a limerick about Python exceptions." } ] output = pipe(messages, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) output[ 0 ][ "generated_text" ][- 1 ] The pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template. Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer . from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer model_id = "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B" tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, dtype= "auto" , device_map= "auto" ) Chat messages = [ { "role" : "system" , "content" : "You should only answer with a number." }, { "role" : "user" , "content" : "What is 17 * 23?" }, ] inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , reasoning_effort= "medium" # by default ).to(model.device) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) tokenizer.parse_response( outputs[ 0 ][input_len:], prefix=inputs[ "input_ids" ][ 0 ] ) Beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see. Tool calling Complete tool-calling example def get_weather ( city: str , unit: str = "celsius" ): """ Get the current weather for a city. Args: city: The city to look up. unit: Temperature unit, "celsius" or "fahrenheit". """ ... tools = [get_weather] messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "I land in Paris tonight. Do I need a coat?" } ] inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, tools=tools, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(model.device) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 1000 ) message = tokenizer.parse_response( outputs[ 0 ][input_len:], prefix=inputs[ "input_ids" ][ 0 ], tools=tools ) message.get( "tool_calls" ) Pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type. Multi-GPU and multi-node Beam's config defines an expert-parallel plan. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig : import os from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B" , distributed_config=DistributedConfig( tp_size= int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]), ep_size= int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]), tp_plan={} ), ) Launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256. vLLM Beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API: vllm serve reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B --tensor-parallel-size 16 --served-model-name beam For faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter: vllm serve reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B \ --tensor-parallel-size 16 \ --speculative-config '{ "method": "dflash", "model": "reflection/dflash2-drafter-preview", "num_speculative_tokens": 15 }' Both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1 . For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM . SGLang Beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s: python -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-NVFP4 \ --served-model-name beam \ --tp 4 \ --attention-backend trtllm_mha \ --page-size 64 \ --context-length 1048576 \ --mem-fraction-static 0.85 \ --enable-unified-memory \ --speculative-algorithm DFLASH \ --speculative-draft-model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-DFlash2 \ --speculative-dflash-block-size 8 \ --tool-call-parser beam --reasoning-parser beam \ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000 On Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses. Below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket . Category Prompt Description Low reasoning (tokens) High reasoning (tokens) Multi-step tool calling Fulfill ORD-742: compare stock, reservations, surcharges and arrival dates; reserve the cheapest eligible warehouse. ✅ 544 ✅ 811 Long-context retrieval over a code base Derive Click command configuration and two invocation results from three complete source files; cite six implementation symbols. 🔴 1,613 * ✅ 5,007 Terminal task in a sandbox Inspect and repair a CSV ledger CLI; fix all bugs, preserve tests, run tests and a CLI check. ✅ 582 ✅ 1,548 Math reasoning (AIME-style) How many eight-element subsets of {1, …, 16} have a sum divisible by 17? Give a justification. 🟠 829 † ✅ 2,809 Structured output Convert an out-of-order revision log into strict JSON: merge patches, cancellations, nulls, dates, currencies and totals. ✅ 1,040 ✅ 2,088 * Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity. † Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed. Don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket , rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit. Post-training Beam You can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. SFT with TRL The quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen. The setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes. After one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself. Training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR . GRPO with Miles Reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can update the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the new weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe. Workload Reference configuration Inference / eval, BF16 16x H200 per engine Full-parameter GRPO, BF16 (Miles) 96x H200: 64 train, 32 rollout. Or 64x H200 colocated. LoRA GRPO, BF16 (Miles) 32x H200: 16 train, 16 rollout. Full-parameter GRPO, BF16, 128-token context (Miles) 48x H200: 32 train, 16 rollout. The setup Reflection and RadixArk first validated on the real checkpoint. The recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes: docker build -f docker/Dockerfile.beam -t miles-beam . python scripts/run_beam.py prepare \ --model-id reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B \ --model-dir /root/models/Beam \ --data-dir /data/datasets export MASTER_ADDR=10.0.0.1 export RAY_ADDRESS=http:// ${MASTER_ADDR} :8265 python scripts/run_beam.py execute \ --model-dir /root/models/Beam \ --data-dir /data/datasets \ --output-dir /root/shared_data/beam-run \ --num-rollout 100 What happens in a rollout: Sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each. Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit. Update: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty. Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute. Optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch. Evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty. The next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one update behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn. Train with LoRA You can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading. python scripts/run_beam_lora.py execute \ --model-dir /root/models/Beam \ --data-dir /data/datasets \ --output-dir /root/shared_data/beam-run \ --num-rollout 100 Build with Beam: Demos If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page . To inspire you, here are a few things we built. Hey Beam, build a native local MacOS application! At Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out. We asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text. Build BeamSpeak, a native macOS menu bar dictation app with a compact recording pill and no main window or account. Use ⌘⇧Space to start and stop microphone recording, showing elapsed time, microphone level, and transcription status. Run speech recognition entirely locally using a Hugging Face model, preferably Parakeet v3 through MLX, and keep the model loaded between recordings. Paste the transcript into the original app if it remains focused and Accessibility permission is granted; otherwise copy it to the clipboard, preserving newer clipboard changes and never pressing Enter. Handle permissions, cancellation, silence, errors, a two-minute recording limit, and temporary audio cleanup. Deliver source code, a runnable BeamSpeak.app, setup instructions, and verification of offline transcription, the physical shortcut, microphone capture, and text delivery. We used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements. You can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace . If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions . Hey Beam, how do you scale on multiple agents? We wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. It is the first model from the new US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens , and is released under the Apache 2.0 license. Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model. Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post shows you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it. TL;DR 501B-parameter MoEs LLM with 23B active per token. 52 layers, 256 experts per MoE layer, 8 routed per token. Text in, text out with context window of 1M tokens. Checkpoint formats: BF16 , FP8 , and NVFP4 Reasoning that can stay in context across turns ( preserve_thinking ), tool calling with a dedicated grammar. The model supports five reasoning values: "low", "medium" (default), "high", "xhigh", and "max". Response template in the tokenizer. Speculative decoding drafter model with DFlash2 Day-0 libraries: transformers, SGLang, vLLM. Full-parameter RL with Miles. Ships with a Rust-based custom harness. Apache 2.0. Build with Beam Reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub: You could make a demo that uses the Beam model on Spaces You could quantize it for your favorite hardware You could generate a synthetic dataset for your favorite problem You could build an RL environment with or for Beam You could benchmark Beam and share the results. You could surprise us! If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page . We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts. What is Beam? Beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one. Attention The decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones. Inside the attention block (both layer types) The two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding . Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1 . It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling. Attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection. Mixture of Experts The first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters. The router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5. Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips. If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below. Residual Stream The residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth. Beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k) . The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state. Every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap. Long Context Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate. Context If all 52 layers were global Beam 32K tokens 6.5 GiB 1.2 GiB 128K tokens 26 GiB 4.6 GiB Full context (1M) 208 GiB 36.08 GiB These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell. A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Plan for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection. Inference Support Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM. Transformers Install the latest version of transformers. pip install -U "transformers>=5.20.1" The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline: from transformers import pipeline pipe = pipeline( "text-generation" , model= "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B" , device_map= "auto" ) messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "Write a limerick about Python exceptions." } ] output = pipe(messages, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) output[ 0 ][ "generated_text" ][- 1 ] The pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template. Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer . from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer model_id = "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B" tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, dtype= "auto" , device_map= "auto" ) Chat messages = [ { "role" : "system" , "content" : "You should only answer with a number." }, { "role" : "user" , "content" : "What is 17 * 23?" }, ] inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , reasoning_effort= "medium" # by default ).to(model.device) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) tokenizer.parse_response( outputs[ 0 ][input_len:], prefix=inputs[ "input_ids" ][ 0 ] ) Beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see. Workload Reference configuration Inference / eval, BF16 16x H200 per engine Full-parameter GRPO, BF16 (Miles) 96x H200: 64 train, 32 rollout. Or 64x H200 colocated. LoRA GRPO, BF16 (Miles) 32x H200: 16 train, 16 rollout. Full-parameter GRPO, BF16, 128-token context (Miles) 48x H200: 32 train, 16 rollout. The setup Reflection and RadixArk first validated on the real checkpoint. The recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes: docker build -f docker/Dockerfile.beam -t miles-beam . python scripts/run_beam.py prepare \ --model-id reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B \ --model-dir /root/models/Beam \ --data-dir /data/datasets export MASTER_ADDR=10.0.0.1 export RAY_ADDRESS=http:// ${MASTER_ADDR} :8265 python scripts/run_beam.py execute \ --model-dir /root/models/Beam \ --data-dir /data/datasets \ --output-dir /root/shared_data/beam-run \ --num-rollout 100 What happens in a rollout: Sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each. Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit. Update: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty. Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute. Optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch. Evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty. The next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one update behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn. Train with LoRA You can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading. python scripts/run_beam_lora.py execute \ --model-dir /root/models/Beam \ --data-dir /data/datasets \ --output-dir /root/shared_data/beam-run \ --num-rollout 100 Build with Beam: Demos If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page . To inspire you, here are a few things we built. Hey Beam, build a native local MacOS application! At Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out. We asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text. Build BeamSpeak, a native macOS menu bar dictation app with a compact recording pill and no main window or account. Use ⌘⇧Space to start and stop microphone recording, showing elapsed time, microphone level, and transcription status. Run speech recognition entirely locally using a Hugging Face model, preferably Parakeet v3 through MLX, and keep the model loaded between recordings. Paste the transcript into the original app if it remains focused and Accessibility permission is granted; otherwise copy it to the clipboard, preserving newer clipboard changes and never pressing Enter. Handle permissions, cancellation, silence, errors, a two-minute recording limit, and temporary audio cleanup. Deliver source code, a runnable BeamSpeak.app, setup instructions, and verification of offline transcription, the physical shortcut, microphone capture, and text delivery. We used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements. You can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace . If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions . Hey Beam, how do you scale on multiple agents? We wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.23830 (cs) [Submitted on 16 Oct 2026] Title: Waiting Buys Exactly Two Moments: Endogenous Identification in Prediction-Driven Allocation Authors: Rama AlHamidi , Rasul Khanbayov , Erchin Serpedin , Hasan Kurban View a PDF of the paper titled Waiting Buys Exactly Two Moments: Endogenous Identification in Prediction-Driven Allocation, by Rama AlHamidi and 3 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: A planner with a fixed budget of preventive help must decide whom to help and when. Waiting reveals risk but removes intervention opportunities as higher-risk individuals leave first. We characterize this tradeoff under repeated noisy signals and risk-dependent attrition: in the canonical model, a length-$\tau$ observation prefix identifies exactly the latent risk moments $m_j=\mathbb E[p^j]$ for $j=0,\ldots,2\tau-1$, buying two new moments per additional period. These identify average next-period attrition among survivors but need not identify allocation welfare or attrition among those prioritized for treatment. Our observationally equivalent constructions establish unavoidable timing regret at any sample size for a fixed observation length, while exact certificates determine whether all compatible populations share a unique optimal date. Matched experiments separate the effects of estimation, bootstrap averaging, and regret weighting. Longer observation often resolves timing ambiguity, but the optimal date may already have passed. In our experiments, bootstrap averaging and early stopping improve decisions, while regret weighting adds no improvement in pooled mean squared regret: better statistical fit need not yield better allocation welfare. The code and artifacts are available at this https URL . Waiting reveals risk but removes intervention opportunities as higher-risk individuals leave first. We characterize this tradeoff under repeated noisy signals and risk-dependent attrition: in the canonical model, a length- τ \tau observation prefix identifies exactly the latent risk moments m j = 𝔼 ⁡ [ p j ] m_{j}=\mathbb{E}[p^{j}] for j = 0 , … , 2 ​ τ − 1 j=0,\ldots,2\tau-1 , buying two new moments per additional period. These identify average next-period attrition among survivors but need not identify allocation welfare or attrition among those prioritized for treatment. Our observationally equivalent constructions establish unavoidable timing regret at any sample size for a fixed observation length, while exact certificates determine whether all compatible populations share a unique optimal date. Matched experiments separate the effects of estimation, bootstrap averaging, and regret weighting. Longer observation often resolves timing ambiguity, but the optimal date may already have passed. In our experiments, bootstrap averaging and early stopping improve decisions, while regret weighting adds no improvement in pooled mean squared regret: better statistical fit need not yield better allocation welfare. The code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/KurbanIntelligenceLab/waiting-buys-two-moments KEYWORDS prediction-driven allocation; allocation timing; partial identification; selective attrition; moment identification; statistical decision theory 1 Introduction Prediction-driven allocation models, such as Novissi [ 1 ] , HPU [ 2 ] , and DEWS [ 3 ] , guide decisions about who should receive support when resources are insufficient to help everyone. For example, consider a hospital with more seriously ill patients than beds equipped to provide close monitoring and life-saving treatment. Doctors can use the information already available to decide who receives those beds, or wait for more test results to better identify who would benefit most. During that wait, however, some patients may become too ill to be saved. Choosing when to act therefore requires weighing the value of additional information against the opportunities to help that disappear during the delay. Figure 1 : Waiting buys exactly two moments, but the riskiest people leave first. After t periods the planner observes exactly the first 2 ​ t − 1 2t-1 moments of the risk distribution (orange tiles), so its reconstruction (orange) of the true distribution (black) sharpens with every period of waiting (blue arrow). The people who generate those clues are the highest-risk ones, and they drop out first (dashed outlines): waiting improves the ranking of a population that has already lost the people most worth helping (red arrow). Our review (Section 2 ) finds that existing timing results characterize when to intervene given the population’s risk distribution [ 4 ] . These results do not address whether a short observation period reveals enough about that distribution to determine whether acting now or waiting would lead to better outcomes. This work closes this gap by establishing what a limited observation period reveals about the population’s risks and whether that information is enough to choose the best intervention date. We show that the observations can reveal how many people are expected to lose their opportunity for help during the next period and establish when these observations determine the best intervention date versus when they leave the decision unresolved. Furthermore, we find that uncertainty about the best time to intervene can persist even when the number of people observed becomes arbitrarily large. This raises a practical question: how do estimation, averaging, and decision criteria affect allocation performance on selected reference populations in this partially identified model? To investigate this question, we compare risk estimation, bootstrap aggregation, and ambiguity-aware decision criteria using simulated populations with known welfare curves. Procedures recommend dates for a future population with the same risk distribution. Comparisons within a common information set isolate the effects of fitting, averaging, and selecting a date. KEY TAKEAWAY Waiting reveals average attrition among survivors, but not whether waiting is worthwhile; identical observations can imply different optimal allocation dates, even with arbitrarily large samples. Our contributions are: 1. Information and timing limits. We characterize the moments revealed by observation, distinguish identified attrition from potentially unidentified welfare, and derive a regret floor that persists at every sample size. 2. Exact decision identification. We reduce comparisons of nonlinear allocation welfare over an infinite-dimensional moment class to two-parameter branch-and-bound with polynomial certificates verified on [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . This certifies a common optimal date or produces an exactly compatible counterexample, for both unrestricted and still-available dates. 3. Decision performance under limited information. We compare risk estimation, bootstrap aggregation, and ambiguity-aware rules. Comparisons holding information fixed show that early stopping can outperform a converged likelihood fit, while regret weighting offers no improvement over ordinary averaging in the reported pooled results. 2 Related work Identification and allocation timing Finite binomial mixtures identify finitely many mixing moments [ 5 , 6 ] , while heterogeneous survival selects those remaining at risk [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] . We characterize what joint signal-and-survival observations identify and the implications for welfare and timing regret. Adopting Shirali et al. [4] ’s model, we ask whether limited observations identify the optimal date across observationally consistent risk distributions; their analysis takes the distribution as given. Their multi-date allocation algorithm is not a directly comparable date-selection baseline: our oracle is optimal only within single-date policies. This complements work on predictive accuracy and allocation design [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] . Decisions under partial identification Welfare and regret criteria under ambiguity are well studied [ 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 ] . We examine how observation and attrition change ambiguity and compare implemented procedures. Existing optimality results require a separate derivation here: Montiel Olea et al. [16] study Gaussian experiments; Kitagawa et al. [17] , binary treatment choice with Gaussian information and interval-identified effects. Our setting uses multinomial signal-and-exit records, allocation-date choices, nonlinear budget-constrained welfare, and squared relative regret normalized by population-optimal welfare. Our CMS bootstrap is therefore an approximate comparison, not an established finite-sample optimal rule. Unlike fixed-estimand sampling [ 18 ] , waiting removes treatment opportunities; unlike strategic disclosure [ 19 ] , information restrictions arise from population dynamics. 3 Problem Setup We adopt the model of Shirali et al. [4] . Individuals have fixed risks p i ​ ∼ iid ​ 𝒫 p_{i}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal{P} on [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] , unknown to the planner. In each period, an active individual produces a warning o i t ∼ Bernoulli ⁡ ( 1 − ( 1 − p i ) γ ) o_{i}^{t}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(1-(1-p_{i})^{\gamma}) and then fails with probability p i p_{i} if untreated. Conditional on risks, signal and failure draws are independent across individuals and periods. Failure permanently removes treatment eligibility. Our main analysis uses γ = 1 \gamma=1 . The planner allocates treatment once before horizon T T , with budget B B covering a fraction β = B / N \beta=B/N of the initial population. At date t t , active individuals are ranked by accumulated warnings y i t = ∑ s = 1 t o i s y_{i}^{t}=\sum_{s=1}^{t}o_{i}^{s} ; treatment proceeds in descending order, uniformly within ties. Treatment prevents failure over the remaining T − t T-t opportunities, giving expected benefit u t ​ ( p ) = 1 − ( 1 − p ) T − t u^{t}(p)=1-(1-p)^{T-t} . Let W t ​ ( 𝒫 , β ) W^{t}(\mathcal{P};\beta) denote the resulting mean-field welfare per initial individual. The earliest optimal date is t ⋆ = min ⁡ arg ​ max t ∈ { 1 , … , T − 1 } ​ W t ​ ( 𝒫 , β ) . t^{\star}=\min\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{t\in\{1,\ldots,T-1\}}W^{t}(\mathcal{P};\beta). Appendix A.1 gives the cohort masses, the treated mass in each warning cohort, and the resulting welfare functional explicitly. We distinguish the observation length τ \tau from the candidate allocation date t t . The theoretical prefix ends after period- τ \tau signals but before that period’s failures. It records earlier failures and warning counts observed while individuals remain active. Cohort counts and exit records restricted to this same window identify the same population features (Appendix A.2 ). Some finite-sample implementations also use period- τ \tau failures; these information differences are stated in Experimental Design. 4 Information and the Limits of Allocation Timing Throughout this section, γ = 1 \gamma=1 and identification refers to exact population observation probabilities. A quantity is identified if it is constant across all risk distributions compatible with those probabilities. Proofs appear in Appendix A . 4.1 What waiting reveals. Lemma 1 (Information accrual) . Let Π d \Pi_{d} denote polynomials of degree at most d d . The observation kernels p ↦ ( s k ) ​ p k ​ ( 1 − p ) 2 ​ s − 1 − k , 1 ≤ s ≤ τ , 0 ≤ k ≤ s , p\mapsto\binom{s}{k}p^{k}(1-p)^{2s-1-k},\qquad 1\leq s\leq\tau,\quad 0\leq k\leq s, span exactly Π 2 ​ τ − 1 \Pi_{2\tau-1} . Hence the population observation probabilities determine moments through degree 2 ​ τ − 1 2\tau-1 and depend only on them. The same holds for exit records restricted to this observation window. The first period identifies mean risk; each additional period reveals two more moments through survivor signals. Attrition removes treatment opportunities while changing what signals reveal. Higher moments need not be identified, though boundary moments can determine the distribution uniquely. Appendix A.5 considers other signal models. 4.2 What the identified moments determine. Proposition 2 (Identification asymmetry) . For a prefix τ ≥ 1 \tau\geq 1 with positive surviving mass, the expected fraction lost during the next untreated period is identified: 𝔼 τ ​ [ p ] = 𝔼 ⁡ [ p ​ ( 1 − p ) τ − 1 ] 𝔼 ⁡ [ ( 1 − p ) τ − 1 ] . \mathbb{E}^{\tau}[p]=\frac{\mathbb{E}[p(1-p)^{\tau-1}]}{\mathbb{E}[(1-p)^{\tau-1}]}. Welfare at date s s involves kernels of degree T + s − 1 T+s-1 and is identified whenever s ≤ 2 ​ τ − T s\leq 2\tau-T . The identified rate measures average survivor attrition, not targeted delay costs: cohort attrition uses degree- 2 ​ τ 2\tau kernels and need not be identified (Appendix A.3 ). The sufficient, not necessary, welfare condition covers no date unless τ ≥ ( T + 1 ) / 2 \tau\geq(T+1)/2 . 4.3 Consequences for timing decisions. For the observed population moments m j = 𝔼 𝒫 ​ [ p j ] m_{j}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}}[p^{j}] , define ℳ τ = { Q a probability distribution on [ 0 , 1 ] : 𝔼 Q [ p j ] = m j , 0 ≤ j ≤ 2 τ − 1 } . \mathcal{M}_{\tau}=\left\{Q\text{ a probability distribution on }[0,1]:\mathbb{E}_{Q}[p^{j}]=m_{j},\quad 0\leq j\leq 2\tau-1\right\}. Uncertain welfare need not imply an uncertain decision: compatible populations may share an optimal date. When they do not, observational equivalence imposes an unavoidable loss. Theorem 3 (Irreducible regret) . For 𝒬 0 , 𝒬 1 ∈ ℳ τ \mathcal{Q}_{0},\mathcal{Q}_{1}\in\mathcal{M}_{\tau} with positive optimal welfare, define R i ​ ( s ) = 1 − W s ​ ( 𝒬 i ) max r ⁡ W r ​ ( 𝒬 i ) , ζ = min s ⁡ { R 0 ​ ( s ) + R 1 ​ ( s ) } , R_{i}(s)=1-\frac{W^{s}(\mathcal{Q}_{i})}{\max_{r}W^{r}(\mathcal{Q}_{i})},\qquad\zeta=\min_{s}\{R_{0}(s)+R_{1}(s)\}, where dates range over { 1 , … , T − 1 } \{1,\ldots,T-1\} . Every rule based on a length- τ \tau prefix, randomized or not, incurs expected relative regret at least ζ / 2 \zeta/2 under at least one population, for every N N . Identical data laws imply identical recommendation distributions. The bound is positive exactly when no optimal date is shared, so larger samples cannot resolve ambiguity at a fixed prefix. 5 Methodology 5.1 Identification ambiguity For the reference population’s unique optimal date d d , we bound each competitor’s largest welfare advantage: V τ ​ ( d , r ) = sup 𝒫 ∈ ℳ τ [ W r ​ ( 𝒫 ) − W d ​ ( 𝒫 ) ] . V_{\tau}(d,r)=\sup_{\mathcal{P}\in\mathcal{M}_{\tau}}[W^{r}(\mathcal{P})-W^{d}(\mathcal{P})]. Strictly negative upper bounds for all r ≠ d r\neq d certify that d d is uniquely optimal throughout ℳ τ \mathcal{M}_{\tau} . A compatible population where a competitor outperforms d d establishes ambiguity: d d fails there, while every other date fails for the reference population. We verify certificates and counterexamples exactly for both unrestricted and still-available dates, leaving unresolved cases undecided. 5.2 Decision performance Each procedure estimates or bounds welfare across dates and recommends an intervention time. Estimators and bootstrap methods We compare certified nonparametric maximum likelihood (NPMLE) [ 6 , 5 ] , a flexible likelihood benchmark; moment-matched Beta [ 4 ] ; and early-stopped expectation–maximization (EM) [ 20 ] , testing whether further likelihood optimization improves decisions. All use d ^ ∈ arg ⁡ max d ​ W d ​ ( 𝒫 ^ ) \hat{d}\in\arg\max_{d}W^{d}(\hat{\mathcal{P}}) ; NPMLE and EM share information, while Beta uses a different observation convention detailed below. Bagged NPMLE [ 21 ] averages bootstrap welfare curves; regret calibration weights the same curves by inverse optimal welfare, isolating regret weighting from averaging. Ambiguity-aware rules We compare four implemented criteria. The achieved-welfare LP selects the earliest candidate date whose approximate best-case achieved welfare is not exceeded by any later date’s approximate worst-case welfare, with extrema taken over a moment confidence region. The worst-case envelope instead compares against next-period best-case full-information welfare, testing whether using achieved welfare changes recommendations. Both scan dates from a fixed observation prefix. Maximin welfare maximizes approximate worst-case achieved welfare. CMS bootstrap adapts the bootstrap decision framework of Christensen et al. [15] to allocation timing, minimizing bootstrap-averaged approximate worst-case regret over distributions matching each draw’s estimated moments, relative to each population’s optimal date. These finite-risk-grid extrema are not full-set certificates, and refinement can change decisions (Appendix C ). 5.3 Evaluation & Data analysis We evaluate recommendations using true population welfare: E = W d ^ ​ ( 𝒫 , β ) / W t ⋆ ​ ( 𝒫 , β ) E=W^{\hat{d}}(\mathcal{P};\beta)/W^{t^{\star}}(\mathcal{P};\beta) and R = 1 − E R=1-E . We report mean squared regret (MSR), the average of R 2 R^{2} , and efficiency’s tenth percentile ( p 10 p_{10} ); lower MSR and higher p 10 p_{10} are better. Displayed MSR is scaled by 10 3 10^{3} , not a percentage. N N controls estimation sample size; evaluation uses mean-field welfare, not realized finite-population allocations. The main comparison retains 1,169 shared runs (589 at N = 10 3 N=10^{3} , 580 at N = 10 5 N=10^{5} ), excluding 31 with missing bagging records. CMS returns all 1,200 decisions, including seven using 19 rather than 20 bootstrap draws. Inference uses paired bootstrap intervals and within-family Holm correction (Appendix C.4 ). Immediate action means date 1 for a future population or date τ \tau when restricted to remaining dates. 6 Experimental Design 6.1 Identification ambiguity Figure 2 : Identical observations, different optimal dates. The two populations have matching observation probabilities through τ = 2 \tau=2 (a), but different welfare curves (b): Q 0 Q_{0} is optimized at s = 5 s=5 , whereas Q 1 Q_{1} is optimized at s = 1 s=1 . The illustrated recommendation s = 5 s=5 is optimal for Q 0 Q_{0} but incurs relative welfare loss under Q 1 Q_{1} . Dates are evaluated as policies for a future population with the same risk distribution. We use 30 configurations formed by crossing five risk distributions—Beta ( 1 , 32 ) (1,32) , Beta ( 1 , 8 ) (1,8) , Beta ( 1 , 4 ) (1,4) , a mixture containing a high-risk subgroup, and a bimodal distribution—with horizons T ∈ { 12 , 20 } T\in\{12,20\} and budget ratios β ∈ { 0.0005 , 0.002 , 0.01 } \beta\in\{0.0005,0.002,0.01\} . We fix γ = 1 \gamma=1 and examine observation lengths τ ∈ { 2 , 3 , 4 } \tau\in\{2,3,4\} , giving 90 configuration–prefix pairs. Each analysis uses exact population moments through degree 2 ​ τ − 1 2\tau-1 , removing sampling error so that any remaining uncertainty reflects identification ambiguity. Indistinguishable populations For each configuration and prefix, we numerically minimize and maximize horizon survival, 𝔼 𝒬 ​ [ ( 1 − p ) T − 1 ] \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{Q}}[(1-p)^{T-1}] , over a moment-matching set on a 2,001-point risk grid. We reconstruct rational weights on the selected supports and verify exact compatibility for all 90 pairs. We then compare their welfare curves and full optimal-date sets and compute the regret lower bound from Theorem 3 in rational arithmetic. These pairs exhibit ambiguity but are not selected to maximize the regret floor. Optimal-date identification For each configuration and prefix, we apply the certification procedure to all dates { 1 , … , T − 1 } \{1,\ldots,T-1\} and separately to available dates { τ , … , T − 1 } \{\tau,\ldots,T-1\} . Certificates cover the full risk interval [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] and are independently verified, together with counterexamples, in exact arithmetic. Among identified available dates, we distinguish immediate action from further waiting. Appendix B.2 details computational budgets. 6.2 Decision performance We use the same 30 population configurations at γ = 1 \gamma=1 , with sample sizes N ∈ { 10 3 , 5 × 10 3 , 2 × 10 4 , 10 5 } N\in\{10^{3},5\times 10^{3},2\times 10^{4},10^{5}\} and observation lengths τ ∈ { 2 , 3 , 4 } \tau\in\{2,3,4\} . Each setting has 20 independent trials, giving 600 planned runs per sample-size–prefix combination. Procedures recommend an allocation date for a future population with the same risk distribution, and recommendations are evaluated using its true welfare curve. Information supplied to each procedure Beta, the two worst-case rules, maximin, and CMS use cohort-based moment estimates through order 2 ​ τ − 1 2\tau-1 , corresponding to the information in the identification experiment. NPMLE, early-stopped EM, bagging, and regret calibration instead use exit records including period- τ \tau failures, revealing one further moment at the population level. Cross-family comparisons therefore reflect differences in both information and procedure. CMS recomputes cohort moments within each bootstrap draw and uses an exact moment-matching set, projecting infeasible estimates when necessary. Maximin and the worst-case rules instead use a covariance-based confidence region. Estimation and bootstrap comparisons We compare certified NPMLE, moment-matched Beta, and EM stopped after 30, 55, or 80 iterations. Bagging and regret calibration share the same retained ensemble from 200 attempted bootstrap fits. Ambiguity-aware comparisons We evaluate the worst-case envelope, achieved-welfare LP, and maximin welfare procedures as numerical approximations, reporting sensitivity to refinement separately from their decision performance. The CMS comparison uses 20 bootstrap draws at τ = 2 \tau=2 and N ∈ { 10 3 , 10 5 } N\in\{10^{3},10^{5}\} , with approximate worst-case regret calculations. Its matched comparison retains 1,169 runs. The estimator comparison at these same sample sizes and prefix retains 1,122 runs across Beta, certified NPMLE, and all three EM stopping counts. Failure handling follows the conventions stated in the evaluation subsection. 7 Results 7.1 Identification ambiguity Table 1 shows that populations with identical observation laws can differ substantially in both welfare and preferred intervention dates. This uncertainty cannot be removed by observing more individuals over the same prefix. Where the constructed pairs have no shared optimal date, Theorem 3 establishes a welfare cost that every observation-based rule must incur under at least one population. Longer observation reduces the exhibited welfare spreads and regret floors, but the two quantities describe different consequences: uncertainty about intervention value need not imply a costly timing mistake. Figure 2 illustrates the disagreement; a date optimal for one compatible population can incur substantial regret under another. The full-set analysis in Table 2 shows that additional observations identify the optimal date in more configurations. Identifying that date does not require identifying the entire risk distribution. It also reveals ambiguity missed by the selected extreme pairs: at τ = 3 \tau=3 , the full-set search finds more ambiguous configurations than the pair construction exhibits. Agreement between two compatible populations therefore cannot establish that a decision is identified. The remaining ambiguous cases at the longest prefix reflect insufficient population information, rather than sampling error or an unresolved computation. In a majority of the identified configuration–prefix cases, the best overall date precedes the observation endpoint. Such knowledge can guide allocation in a future population, but cannot recover a missed opportunity in the observed one. The available-date panel of Table 2 addresses the remaining decision directly. Restricting the options can resolve disagreement about past dates; among the resulting identified decisions, acting now is much more common than waiting further. Thus, on this benchmark, additional information often settles when to stop waiting, while some populations remain indistinguishable even about the best action still available.
