Affiliation: KAIST Affiliation: Helmholtz Munich Hyesu Lim Affiliation: Helmholtz Munich Jaegul Choo Affiliation: KAIST Steffen Schneider † † thanks: Correspondence: steffen.schneider@helmholtz-munich.de Affiliation: Helmholtz Munich Abstract Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) explain foundation model representations by decomposing activations into sparse combinations of learned dictionary atoms. However, the learned dictionaries can vary across training runs, limiting the reliability and reproducibility of SAE-based analyses. We propose Consistent Sparse Dictionary Learning (ConSDL), which replaces the standard linear encoder with per-sample sparse coding. This is motivated by our synthetic analysis showing that coefficients from a single linear encoder pass are suboptimal compared with those obtained by per-sample optimization, suggesting that sparse coding is a reliable mechanism for dictionary learning. Across 16 synthetic settings, ConSDL achieves near-perfect dictionary and coefficient recovery. These gains translate to state-of-the-art cross-seed consistency across four vision and language settings, where ConSDL improves dictionary and coefficient consistency by 17.6% and 35.9%, respectively, over the average of six SAE baselines. Code | Weights | Project Page 1 Introduction Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) ( Cunningham et al., 2023 ) have become a widely used approach for analyzing the internal representations of foundation models. SAEs decompose each model activation into a sparse linear combination of vectors from a learned overcomplete dictionary. Empirically, these dictionary vectors often align with human-interpretable concepts, such as colors, textures, and objects in vision models ( Thasarathan et al., 2025 ) or characters, words, and syntactic patterns in language models ( Elhage et al., 2022 ; Bricken et al., 2023 ) . Importantly, these concepts can be learned without a predefined vocabulary, enabling scalable explanations of model behavior in vision ( Lim et al., 2025 ; Pach et al., 2026 ) and language ( Templeton et al., 2026 ) , audits of hidden biases in models and datasets ( Ahsan and Wallace, 2025 ; Choi et al., 2026 ) , and identification of candidate factors in scientific and medical data ( Dasdelen et al., 2025 ; Nerrise et al., 2026 ) . Yet, a critical limitation remains before SAEs can serve as practical tools for analysis. SAEs trained on the same data with the same configuration can learn substantially different dictionaries across random seeds ( Paulo and Belrose, 2025 ) . This limits reproducibility and reliability. More fundamentally, it raises the question of whether the features learned by SAEs genuinely reflect the model’s internal representations or are artifacts of the training procedure. Recent work has further heightened this concern by showing that SAEs can fail to recover known ground-truth features in controlled synthetic settings ( Korznikov et al., 2026 ; Pacela et al., 2026 ) . In this paper, we propose Consistent Sparse Dictionary Learning (ConSDL) to make sparse decompositions of model activations consistent across independent training runs, enabling reliable and reproducible analysis. To this end, ConSDL replaces the linear encoder of SAEs with per-sample sparse coding. The algorithm design is motivated by prior work showing that coefficients predicted by a single encoder pass can be suboptimal compared with those obtained by per-sample optimization ( O’Neill et al., 2024 ) . We hypothesize that updating the dictionary with these suboptimal coefficients contributes to inconsistency across training runs. ConSDL therefore uses per-sample sparse coding throughout training to obtain coefficients before each dictionary update. To make this procedure stable in practice, we additionally use coefficient refitting to correct shrinkage from the sparsity penalty and a co-active similarity regularizer to reduce dictionary redundancy. Across diverse synthetic and real-world settings, ConSDL consistently outperforms existing SAEs. In controlled synthetic experiments, ConSDL achieves near-perfect recovery of ground-truth dictionaries and coefficients, even with larger dictionaries and highly imbalanced atom-selection probabilities, where existing methods degrade. These results support our hypothesis that improved coefficient estimation leads to more consistent dictionary learning. ConSDL substantially improves dictionary and coefficient consistency over existing methods on vision and language foundation models. Our contributions are threefold. First, we introduce ConSDL, which incorporates per-sample sparse coding to produce consistent sparse decompositions across training runs. Second, we systematically study SAE recovery under synthetic conditions and identify when existing methods fail and what factors contribute to these failures. Third, we show that ConSDL improves cross-seed dictionary and coefficient consistency on foundation-model activations across multiple vision and language backbones, dictionary widths, and sparsity levels. 2 Related work Consistency of SAEs. Recent work has drawn attention to the inconsistency of SAEs, showing that independent training runs can learn substantially different dictionaries ( Paulo and Belrose, 2025 ) . Fel et al. (2025) improve dictionary consistency by constraining dictionary atoms to lie within the convex hull of the activation data. Nelson et al. (2026b) instead regularizes the dictionary geometry to reduce ambiguity among sparse codes, improving dictionary and coefficient consistency. However, these studies differ in key experimental choices, including dictionary size, sparsity, and training procedure, making direct comparison difficult. Song et al. (2025) further show that SAE consistency can vary substantially across such configurations. It therefore remains unclear whether the reported gains hold under matched settings. We address this by comparing existing methods across a broad range of settings using the same evaluation protocol. Sparse coding and dictionary learning. Given a fixed dictionary, sparse coding infers a sparse coefficient to reconstruct each input as a linear combination of dictionary codes ( Olshausen and Field, 1997 ) . A common formulation uses an ℓ 1 \ell_{1} penalty and can be solved with ISTA ( Daubechies et al., 2004 ) or its accelerated variant FISTA ( Beck and Teboulle, 2009 ) , while LISTA ( Gregor and LeCun, 2010 ) unrolls ISTA into a fixed-depth network with learned parameters for faster inference. Alternatively, matching pursuit greedily selects atoms that best explain the current residual ( Mallat and Zhang, 1993 ) . Dictionary learning jointly learns the dictionary by alternating between sparse coefficient estimation and dictionary updates ( Aharon et al., 2006 ; Mairal et al., 2010 ) . Our proposed ConSDL adopts this alternating formulation, using FISTA for per-sample sparse inference before each dictionary update. Under suitable assumptions, such iterative approaches are theoretically guaranteed to recover the underlying dictionary and coefficients ( Agarwal et al., 2016 ) . From amortized inference to per-sample sparse coding. Standard SAEs use a shared learned encoder to predict sparse coefficients rather than optimizing them separately for each input. This amortized inference ( Marino et al., 2018 ) avoids costly per-sample optimization and enables efficient large-scale training, but at a cost to coefficient quality. O’Neill et al. (2024) show that optimizing coefficients directly under a fixed dictionary substantially improves recovery. Sun et al. (2026) connect amortized inference to feature absorption, splitting, and dead atoms. Joung and Bae (2026) retain an amortized encoder but iteratively refine its predicted coefficients during dictionary learning. Pacela et al. (2026) instead remove the learned encoder and use per-sample sparse coding throughout training, but report degraded recovery for larger dictionaries. Our ConSDL builds on this non-amortized approach while improving its stability and scalability to foundation-model activations. Recovery guarantees for sparse coding and dictionary learning Sparse recovery theory characterizes when the underlying coefficients can be recovered from observations generated by a known dictionary ( Donoho and Elad, 2003 ; Candes et al., 2006 ) . Exact recovery is possible when coefficients are sufficiently sparse and the dictionary atoms are sufficiently distinct, so that different sparse codes do not produce the same observation ( Donoho and Elad, 2003 ) . Restricted isometry provides a stronger formal condition by requiring the dictionary to approximately preserve the geometry of sparse vectors ( Candes et al., 2006 ) . When the dictionary is also unknown, the problem additionally requires identifying the dictionary from multiple sparse observations. Under suitable assumptions, including sufficient observations and an initialization close to the ground-truth dictionary, alternating minimization can recover both an overcomplete dictionary and its coefficients ( Agarwal et al., 2016 ) . Additional related work is discussed in Appendix A . 3 Method We propose Consistent Sparse Dictionary Learning (ConSDL) to improve the consistency of dictionaries and coefficients across training runs (Fig. 1 ). ConSDL replaces the learned encoder with per-input coefficient optimization and updates the dictionary from these estimates. It then refits the magnitudes of the selected coefficients without the sparsity penalty to correct shrinkage from sparse coding, and encourages distinct co-active atoms by penalizing the similarity of the most similar co-active pair. 3.1 Per-sample Sparse Coding Figure 1: Method. Left : Consistent Sparse Dictionary Learning (ConSDL) alternates between per-sample sparse coefficient inference with refitting and decoder updates under a reconstruction objective with co-active similarity regularization, holding the other component fixed at each stage. Standard SAEs (inset) instead use a learned encoder trained jointly with the decoder. Stacked panels indicate independent training seeds, across which ConSDL aims to recover consistent codes and dictionaries. Right : Python-style pseudocode. Let 𝐱 ∈ ℝ d \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denote a model activation with dimension d d , which we aim to decompose into a linear combination of m m dictionary atoms weighted by non-negative, sparse coefficient vector. Let W dec ∈ ℝ d × m W_{\mathrm{dec}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m} denote the learned dictionary, corresponding to the decoder weight in an SAE. Its j j -th column 𝐰 j ∈ ℝ d \mathbf{w}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} represents a unit-norm dictionary atom. Let 𝐛 dec ∈ ℝ d \mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{dec}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denote the decoder bias, and 𝐚 ∈ ℝ ≥ 0 m \mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{m} denote the nonnegative coefficient vector, with a j ∈ ℝ a_{j}\in\mathbb{R} specifying the contribution of atom j j to the reconstruction. Standard SAEs use a linear encoder followed by a non-linearity to predict the sparse coefficients 𝐚 \mathbf{a} from each input in a single forward pass. These coefficients directly influence the gradients used to update each dictionary atom during training, yet coefficients produced by a single encoder pass can be suboptimal compared with those optimized for the current dictionary ( O’Neill et al., 2024 ) . We therefore replace the encoder in a conventional SAE with per-sample sparse coding and infer the coefficients for each input as the solution to the optimization problem: 𝐚 sc ​ ( 𝐱 ) = arg ​ min 𝐚 ≥ 0 ⁡ 1 2 ​ ‖ 𝐱 − W dec ​ 𝐚 − 𝐛 dec ‖ 2 2 + λ ​ ‖ 𝐚 ‖ 1 , \mathbf{a}^{\mathrm{sc}}(\mathbf{x})=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\mathbf{a}\geq 0}\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathbf{x}-W_{\mathrm{dec}}\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{dec}}\right\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda\|\mathbf{a}\|_{1}, (1) where λ > 0 \lambda>0 controls the sparsity penalty. We estimate the solution using the Fast Iterative Shrinkage-Thresholding Algorithm (FISTA; Beck and Teboulle, 2009 ). Each FISTA iteration updates the coefficients by taking a gradient step on the reconstruction term, followed by nonnegative soft thresholding for the ℓ 1 \ell_{1} penalty. 3.2 Coefficient Refitting While the ℓ 1 \ell_{1} penalty promotes sparsity by penalizing coefficient magnitude, it also introduces shrinkage bias : even after the active atoms are correctly identified, the optimization objective favors smaller nonzero coefficients to reduce the penalty ( Zou, 2006 ) . Using these shrunken coefficients directly for decoder updates can underestimate the contributions of the selected atoms ( Tolooshams and Ba, 2021 ) . We therefore retain the nonzero coefficients identified by FISTA and refit them without the ℓ 1 \ell_{1} penalty, following post-selection refitting procedures in sparse estimation ( Figueiredo et al., 2007 ; Chzhen et al., 2019 ) . Collecting the indices of non-zero coefficients in the support S sc ​ ( 𝐱 ) = { j : a j sc ​ ( 𝐱 ) > 0 } S^{\mathrm{sc}}(\mathbf{x})=\{j:a_{j}^{\mathrm{sc}}(\mathbf{x})>0\} , we solve 𝐚 refit ​ ( 𝐱 ) = arg ​ min a j ​ ∀ j ∈ S sc ​ ( 𝐱 ) ⁡ 1 2 ​ ‖ 𝐱 − W dec ​ 𝐚 − 𝐛 dec ‖ 2 2 , \mathbf{a}^{\mathrm{refit}}(\mathbf{x})=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\begin{subarray}{c}a_{j}\forall j\in S^{\mathrm{sc}}(\mathbf{x})\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathbf{x}-W_{\mathrm{dec}}\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{dec}}\right\|_{2}^{2}, (2) using projected gradient descent initialized from 𝐚 sc ​ ( 𝐱 ) \mathbf{a}^{\mathrm{sc}}(\mathbf{x}) , constraining the coefficients to remain nonnegative and supported on S sc ​ ( 𝐱 ) S^{\mathrm{sc}}(\mathbf{x}) . Thus, refitting adjusts only the magnitudes of the selected coefficients without activating new atoms. Additional details on the FISTA optimization and refitting procedure are provided in Appendix B . 3.3 Co-active Similarity Regularization Per-sample sparse coding improves coefficient estimation, but applying it throughout dictionary learning can still lead multiple atoms to converge to similar directions, resulting in redundant dictionary elements. To stabilize dictionary learning in practice, we introduce a co-active similarity regularizer that penalizes high similarity only between atoms active for the same sample, rather than between all atom pairs in the dictionary. For each input 𝐱 i \mathbf{x}_{i} , let A i = { 𝐰 j : a i , j refit > 0 } A_{i}=\{\mathbf{w}_{j}:a_{i,j}^{\mathrm{refit}}>0\} denote the set of active dictionary atoms, where j j refers to the atom index. For each 𝐰 j ∈ A i \mathbf{w}_{j}\in A_{i} , we define its most similar co-active atom as 𝐰 ~ i , j = arg ​ max 𝐰 ∈ A i ∖ { 𝐰 j } ⁡ 𝐰 j ⊤ ​ 𝐰 , s i , j = 𝐰 j ⊤ ​ 𝐰 ~ i , j . \widetilde{\mathbf{w}}_{i,j}=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\mathbf{w}\in A_{i}\setminus\{\mathbf{w}_{j}\}}\mathbf{w}_{j}^{\top}\mathbf{w},\qquad s_{i,j}=\mathbf{w}_{j}^{\top}\widetilde{\mathbf{w}}_{i,j}. (3) where s i , j s_{i,j} is their cosine similarity, since the atoms are unit normalized. To focus the regularization on highly similar pairs, we follow margin-based contrastive objectives ( Hadsell et al., 2006 ) and formulate the co-active similarity penalty as ℒ sim = 1 | 𝒱 μ | ​ ∑ ( i , j ) ∈ 𝒱 μ ( s i , j − μ ) 2 , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sim}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}_{\mu}|}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{V}_{\mu}}\left(s_{i,j}-\mu\right)^{2}, (4) where μ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ) \mu\in[0,1) is a similarity margin and 𝒱 μ = { ( i , j ) : 𝐰 j ∈ A i , s i , j > μ } \mathcal{V}_{\mu}=\{(i,j):\mathbf{w}_{j}\in A_{i},\ s_{i,j}>\mu\} is the set of matched co-active pairs whose similarity exceeds the margin. Implementation details of the regularizer are provided in Appendix B . 3.4 Training Objective and Alternating Optimization Given the refitted coefficients, we define the reconstruction loss as ℒ rec = 1 2 ​ ‖ 𝐱 − W dec ​ 𝐚 refit ​ ( 𝐱 ) − 𝐛 dec ‖ 2 2 . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}=\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathbf{x}-W_{\mathrm{dec}}\mathbf{a}^{\mathrm{refit}}(\mathbf{x})-\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{dec}}\right\|_{2}^{2}. (5) The overall training objective is ℒ = ℒ rec + γ sim ​ ℒ sim , \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}+\gamma_{\mathrm{sim}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sim}}, where γ sim > 0 \gamma_{\mathrm{sim}}>0 controls the strength of co-active similarity regularization. For each update, we first infer and refit the coefficients under the current dictionary and identify the co-active atom pairs. These quantities are then held fixed while optimizing W dec W_{\mathrm{dec}} and 𝐛 dec \mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{dec}} . Thus, gradients do not propagate through coefficient estimation or pair selection, and training alternates between per-sample sparse coding and dictionary updates. Full optimization details are provided in Appendix B , with hyperparameter settings in Appendix D . Figure 2: Synthetic recovery and cross-seed consistency. (A) Activations are generated from a ground-truth dictionary W GT W_{\mathrm{GT}} with sparse codes a GT \mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{GT}} . Insets show the sampling distributions for the active-set size, coefficient magnitudes, and atom selection frequencies. (B) Dictionary ( DCS ; upper-left) and coefficient ( MCC ; lower-right) recovery across dictionary sizes and tail exponents β \beta . (C) Cross-seed consistency correlates with ground-truth recovery for both dictionaries (top) and coefficients (bottom). Each point is one method at a given dictionary size and β \beta . r r and ρ \rho denote the Pearson and Spearman correlation coefficients. 4 Synthetic Analysis of Dictionary and Coefficient Recovery To study the conditions under which existing SAE methods recover the underlying dictionary and coefficients, and whether ConSDL improves recovery where they fail, we use controlled synthetic data with a known ground-truth decomposition. 4.1 Experimental Setup Synthetic data generation. We generate synthetic data as 𝐱 = ∑ i = 1 m a i ​ 𝐰 i , \mathbf{x}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}a_{i}\mathbf{w}_{i}, where 𝐱 ∈ ℝ d \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is an observed activation, 𝐰 i ∈ ℝ d \mathbf{w}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denotes a ground-truth dictionary atom, and a i ∈ ℝ ≥ 0 a_{i}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} is its nonnegative coefficient. In the baseline setting, we use activation dimension d = 768 d=768 , dictionary width m = 3072 m=3072 , and an expected k=60 active atoms per sample (Fig. 2 A). Following prior synthetic SAE studies ( Korznikov et al., 2026 ; O’Neill et al., 2024 ) , we sample dictionary atoms independently from an isotropic Gaussian distribution and normalize them to unit norm. For each sample, atoms are selected independently with equal probability, yielding random sparse supports over an approximately incoherent dictionary, as commonly assumed in sparse coding analyses ( Arora et al., 2015 ) . Each nonzero coefficient is drawn from a log-normal distribution with expected value 1 1 . We extend the baseline setting along two axes motivated by properties of foundation-model representations: dictionary size and atom-selection imbalance. First, we vary the ground-truth dictionary width over 4 × 4\times , 8 × 8\times , 12 × 12\times , and 16 × 16\times the activation dimension, corresponding to m = 3072 m=3072 – 12288 12288 . This range reflects evidence that larger dictionaries continue to uncover additional concepts in foundation model activations ( Templeton et al., 2026 ) . Second, we vary atom-selection imbalance using Zipf exponents β ∈ { 0 , 0.5 , 0.7 , 1.0 } \beta\in\{0,0.5,0.7,1.0\} , where β = 0 \beta=0 corresponds to uniform selection and larger values produce increasingly long-tailed frequencies, reflecting the highly imbalanced concept frequencies in web-scale pretraining data ( Udandarao et al., 2024 ) . This results in 16 synthetic configurations. Baselines. We compare a standard ReLU SAE ( Cunningham et al., 2023 ) with TopK ( Gao et al., 2025 ) , BatchTopK ( Bussmann et al., 2024 ) , Matryoshka SAE ( Bussmann et al., 2025 ) , MP-SAE ( Costa et al., 2026 ) , and iSAE ( Hindupur et al., 2026 ) . For each synthetic configuration, we generate 10 6 10^{6} observations and train each method for five epochs, reducing the likelihood that recovery failures arise from insufficient data or training. We repeat each experiment with three random seeds. Metrics. We evaluate dictionary recovery using decoder cosine similarity ( DCS ) ( Paulo and Belrose, 2025 ) after Hungarian matching to the ground-truth dictionary. Coefficient recovery is measured by mean coefficient correlation ( MCC ) ( Pacela et al., 2026 ) under the same matching. For cross-seed consistency, we apply the same metrics between independently trained runs and average over all seed pairs. Higher values indicate better recovery or consistency. Full metric definitions and experimental details are provided in Appendix D . 4.2 Findings Table 1: Per-sample re-optimization improves coefficient recovery under a fixed dictionary. Under uniform atom-selection frequencies ( β = 0 \beta=0 ), we compare amortized coefficients with per-sample FISTA re-optimization using fixed trained decoders. Darker green indicates larger improvements over amortized inference. Architecture # Atoms DCS ℓ 0 \ell_{0} MCC Input R 2 R^{2} Amortized Re-optimized Amortized Re-optimized Amortized Re-optimized ReLU 3K 0.983 67.4 63.8 0.833 0.975 0.659 0.885 6K 0.970 76.5 75.6 0.780 0.962 0.633 0.872 9K 0.777 62.5 92.8 0.555 0.672 0.434 0.585 12K 0.367 86.9 70.6 0.157 0.168 0.268 0.249 TopK 3K 0.982 60.0 60.0 0.862 0.947 0.812 0.920 6K 0.810 60.0 60.0 0.611 0.669 0.646 0.699 9K 0.227 60.0 60.0 0.048 0.048 0.403 0.427 12K 0.181 60.0 60.0 0.023 0.023 0.400 0.423 Recovery strongly depends on the data setting. Despite differences across SAE variants, dictionary and coefficient recovery are generally high for smaller dictionaries and less long-tailed atom selection distributions (lower-left region of each heatmap in Fig. 2 B). As dictionary size grows and atom selection becomes more long-tailed, both decline sharply (upper-right region). This sensitivity may help explain why prior synthetic studies have reported both successful ( Song et al., 2025 ) and failed ( Pacela et al., 2026 ) SAE recovery. Since it is unclear which setting best reflects real model activations, these results motivate methods that remain reliable across a wider range of conditions. Amortization gap in coefficient inference. Even in settings with high dictionary recovery, the encoder does not fully recover the corresponding coefficients. One possible explanation is the amortization gap identified in prior work ( O’Neill et al., 2024 ) . We examine this by re-optimizing the coefficients for each sample while keeping the learned dictionary fixed. This improves both coefficient recovery and input reconstruction (Table 1 and 7 ), showing that the encoder leaves recoverable error in coefficient inference. However, when dictionary recovery is poor, coefficient re-optimization yields limited gains, suggesting that a more fundamental solution requires reliable dictionary learning. ConSDL remains robust under challenging synthetic conditions. Across all 16 synthetic settings, ConSDL achieves near-perfect recovery of both the ground-truth coefficients and dictionary, including conditions where existing SAE methods degrade (Fig. 2 B). This shows that incorporating per-sample sparse coding into dictionary learning not only addresses the coefficient-inference gap, but also improves dictionary recovery when incorporated into dictionary learning. By recovering nearly the same ground-truth decomposition across runs, ConSDL also achieves high cross-seed consistency. Full results are provided in Appendix E (Tables 11 – 14 ). Cross-seed consistency is associated with ground-truth recovery. Across the synthetic sweeps, higher cross-seed consistency corresponds to stronger ground-truth recovery (Fig. 2 C). SAEs decompose each model activation into a sparse linear combination of vectors from a learned overcomplete dictionary. Empirically, these dictionary vectors often align with human-interpretable concepts, such as colors, textures, and objects in vision models ( Thasarathan et al., 2025 ) or characters, words, and syntactic patterns in language models ( Elhage et al., 2022 ; Bricken et al., 2023 ) . Importantly, these concepts can be learned without a predefined vocabulary, enabling scalable explanations of model behavior in vision ( Lim et al., 2025 ; Pach et al., 2026 ) and language ( Templeton et al., 2026 ) , audits of hidden biases in models and datasets ( Ahsan and Wallace, 2025 ; Choi et al., 2026 ) , and identification of candidate factors in scientific and medical data ( Dasdelen et al., 2025 ; Nerrise et al., 2026 ) . Yet, a critical limitation remains before SAEs can serve as practical tools for analysis. SAEs trained on the same data with the same configuration can learn substantially different dictionaries across random seeds ( Paulo and Belrose, 2025 ) . This limits reproducibility and reliability. More fundamentally, it raises the question of whether the features learned by SAEs genuinely reflect the model’s internal representations or are artifacts of the training procedure. Recent work has further heightened this concern by showing that SAEs can fail to recover known ground-truth features in controlled synthetic settings ( Korznikov et al., 2026 ; Pacela et al., 2026 ) . In this paper, we propose Consistent Sparse Dictionary Learning (ConSDL) to make sparse decompositions of model activations consistent across independent training runs, enabling reliable and reproducible analysis. To this end, ConSDL replaces the linear encoder of SAEs with per-sample sparse coding. The algorithm design is motivated by prior work showing that coefficients predicted by a single encoder pass can be suboptimal compared with those obtained by per-sample optimization ( O’Neill et al., 2024 ) . We hypothesize that updating the dictionary with these suboptimal coefficients contributes to inconsistency across training runs. ConSDL therefore uses per-sample sparse coding throughout training to obtain coefficients before each dictionary update. To make this procedure stable in practice, we additionally use coefficient refitting to correct shrinkage from the sparsity penalty and a co-active similarity regularizer to reduce dictionary redundancy. Across diverse synthetic and real-world settings, ConSDL consistently outperforms existing SAEs. In controlled synthetic experiments, ConSDL achieves near-perfect recovery of ground-truth dictionaries and coefficients, even with larger dictionaries and highly imbalanced atom-selection probabilities, where existing methods degrade. These results support our hypothesis that improved coefficient estimation leads to more consistent dictionary learning. ConSDL substantially improves dictionary and coefficient consistency over existing methods on vision and language foundation models. Our contributions are threefold. First, we introduce ConSDL, which incorporates per-sample sparse coding to produce consistent sparse decompositions across training runs. Second, we systematically study SAE recovery under synthetic conditions and identify when existing methods fail and what factors contribute to these failures. Third, we show that ConSDL improves cross-seed dictionary and coefficient consistency on foundation-model activations across multiple vision and language backbones, dictionary widths, and sparsity levels. 2 Related work Consistency of SAEs. Recent work has drawn attention to the inconsistency of SAEs, showing that independent training runs can learn substantially different dictionaries ( Paulo and Belrose, 2025 ) . Fel et al. (2025) improve dictionary consistency by constraining dictionary atoms to lie within the convex hull of the activation data. Nelson et al. (2026b) instead regularizes the dictionary geometry to reduce ambiguity among sparse codes, improving dictionary and coefficient consistency. However, these studies differ in key experimental choices, including dictionary size, sparsity, and training procedure, making direct comparison difficult. Song et al. (2025) further show that SAE consistency can vary substantially across such configurations. It therefore remains unclear whether the reported gains hold under matched settings. We address this by comparing existing methods across a broad range of settings using the same evaluation protocol. Sparse coding and dictionary learning. Given a fixed dictionary, sparse coding infers a sparse coefficient to reconstruct each input as a linear combination of dictionary codes ( Olshausen and Field, 1997 ) . A common formulation uses an ℓ 1 \ell_{1} penalty and can be solved with ISTA ( Daubechies et al., 2004 ) or its accelerated variant FISTA ( Beck and Teboulle, 2009 ) , while LISTA ( Gregor and LeCun, 2010 ) unrolls ISTA into a fixed-depth network with learned parameters for faster inference. Alternatively, matching pursuit greedily selects atoms that best explain the current residual ( Mallat and Zhang, 1993 ) . Dictionary learning jointly learns the dictionary by alternating between sparse coefficient estimation and dictionary updates ( Aharon et al., 2006 ; Mairal et al., 2010 ) . Our proposed ConSDL adopts this alternating formulation, using FISTA for per-sample sparse inference before each dictionary update. Under suitable assumptions, such iterative approaches are theoretically guaranteed to recover the underlying dictionary and coefficients ( Agarwal et al., 2016 ) . From amortized inference to per-sample sparse coding. Standard SAEs use a shared learned encoder to predict sparse coefficients rather than optimizing them separately for each input. This amortized inference ( Marino et al., 2018 ) avoids costly per-sample optimization and enables efficient large-scale training, but at a cost to coefficient quality. O’Neill et al. (2024) show that optimizing coefficients directly under a fixed dictionary substantially improves recovery. Sun et al. (2026) connect amortized inference to feature absorption, splitting, and dead atoms. Joung and Bae (2026) retain an amortized encoder but iteratively refine its predicted coefficients during dictionary learning. Pacela et al. (2026) instead remove the learned encoder and use per-sample sparse coding throughout training, but report degraded recovery for larger dictionaries. Our ConSDL builds on this non-amortized approach while improving its stability and scalability to foundation-model activations. Recovery guarantees for sparse coding and dictionary learning Sparse recovery theory characterizes when the underlying coefficients can be recovered from observations generated by a known dictionary ( Donoho and Elad, 2003 ; Candes et al., 2006 ) . Exact recovery is possible when coefficients are sufficiently sparse and the dictionary atoms are sufficiently distinct, so that different sparse codes do not produce the same observation ( Donoho and Elad, 2003 ) . Restricted isometry provides a stronger formal condition by requiring the dictionary to approximately preserve the geometry of sparse vectors ( Candes et al., 2006 ) . When the dictionary is also unknown, the problem additionally requires identifying the dictionary from multiple sparse observations. Under suitable assumptions, including sufficient observations and an initialization close to the ground-truth dictionary, alternating minimization can recover both an overcomplete dictionary and its coefficients ( Agarwal et al., 2016 ) . Additional related work is discussed in Appendix A . 3 Method We propose Consistent Sparse Dictionary Learning (ConSDL) to improve the consistency of dictionaries and coefficients across training runs (Fig. 1 ). ConSDL replaces the learned encoder with per-input coefficient optimization and updates the dictionary from these estimates. It then refits the magnitudes of the selected coefficients without the sparsity penalty to correct shrinkage from sparse coding, and encourages distinct co-active atoms by penalizing the similarity of the most similar co-active pair. 3.1 Per-sample Sparse Coding Figure 1: Method. Left : Consistent Sparse Dictionary Learning (ConSDL) alternates between per-sample sparse coefficient inference with refitting and decoder updates under a reconstruction objective with co-active similarity regularization, holding the other component fixed at each stage. Standard SAEs (inset) instead use a learned encoder trained jointly with the decoder. This range reflects evidence that larger dictionaries continue to uncover additional concepts in foundation model activations ( Templeton et al., 2026 ) . This results in 16 synthetic configurations. Baselines. We compare a standard ReLU SAE ( Cunningham et al., 2023 ) with TopK ( Gao et al., 2025 ) , BatchTopK ( Bussmann et al., 2024 ) , Matryoshka SAE ( Bussmann et al., 2025 ) , MP-SAE ( Costa et al., 2026 ) , and iSAE ( Hindupur et al., 2026 ) . We evaluate dictionary recovery using decoder cosine similarity ( DCS ) ( Paulo and Belrose, 2025 ) after Hungarian matching to the ground-truth dictionary. Coefficient recovery is measured by mean coefficient correlation ( MCC ) ( Pacela et al., 2026 ) under the same matching. For cross-seed consistency, we apply the same metrics between independently trained runs and average over all seed pairs. Higher values indicate better recovery or consistency. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.23796 (cs) [Submitted on 16 Oct 2026] Title: FuTransformer: FP8 prefill and INT4 decode for Llama-style inference on Hopper Authors: Wei Wang View a PDF of the paper titled FuTransformer: FP8 prefill and INT4 decode for Llama-style inference on Hopper, by Wei Wang View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Transformer prefill reuses weights across tokens and is dominated by matrix multiplication and activation data movement; single-token decode has limited reuse and is dominated by weight and KV-cache reads. We present FUTRANSFORMER, a CUDA implementation of a Llama-style Transformer block for NVIDIA Hopper GPUs. It applies CODA's GEMM-plus-epilogue approach to inference, adding direct KV-cache placement, folding the fixed RMSNorm gain into weights, writing FP8 output directly with delayed scaling, and supporting prefill without padding. Decode uses INT4 projection weights and an INT4 KV-cache copy. Weights and keys follow Tensor Core fragment layouts for direct dequantization into MMA operands without full intermediate tiles. A block-diagonal Hadamard transform reduces cache quantization error from outlier channels. On one H100, prefill is up to 1.48x faster than compiled PyTorch FP8 and reaches 1.29 PFLOP/s. For gate/up projection with SwiGLU at the 8B shape, our BF16 path is 1.13x faster than CODA. Our FP8 path is 2.02-2.18x faster than the evaluated BF16 CODA path. Across 8B and 70B shapes at batches 1-32, INT4 decode is 1.3-2.4x faster than the faster of PyTorch's BF16 and INT4 blocks at each point: 2.1-3.3x faster than compiled, CUDA-graphed BF16 and 1.3-6.3x faster than the same block using PyTorch's INT4 projection kernel, which targets a single query row and loses to BF16 at batch 32. It is also 31-51% faster than our FP8 path. Complete Llama-3.1-8B decode takes 2.8 ms per step at batch one, versus 8.1 ms for the compiled transformers implementation. Decoding every WikiText-2 token through the INT4 weight path raises perplexity from 6.24 to 7.23 with round-to-nearest weights or 6.99 with GPTQ in the same format; the rotated INT4 cache adds 0.20. The kernels match a quantized reference computation within 0.001 perplexity. It is also 31-51% faster than our FP8 path. Complete Llama-3.1-8B decode takes 2.8 ms per step at batch one, versus 8.1 ms for the compiled transformers implementation. Decoding every WikiText-2 token through the INT4 weight path raises perplexity from 6.24 to 7.23 with round-to-nearest weights or 6.99 with GPTQ in the same format; the rotated INT4 cache adds 0.20. The kernels match a quantized reference computation within 0.001 perplexity. FuTransformer: FP8 Prefill and INT4 Decode for Llama-Style Inference on Hopper Wei Wang wei.wang217@gmail.com † † footnotetext: Correspondence to: Wei Wang <wei.wang217@gmail.com>. Abstract Transformer inference has different bottlenecks during prefill and decode. Prefill reuses weights across many tokens and is dominated by matrix multiplication and activation data movement. Single-token decode has limited data reuse and is dominated by weight and KV-cache reads. We present FuTransformer , a CUDA implementation of a Llama-style Transformer block for NVIDIA Hopper GPUs. CODA showed how to express Transformer training operators as GEMM-plus-epilogue programs. FuTransformer applies this principle to inference. It adds direct KV-cache placement, folds the fixed RMSNorm gain into weights, writes FP8 values directly from the producing epilogue using delayed scaling, and supports prefill without padding. For decode, FuTransformer uses INT4 projection weights and an INT4 copy of the KV cache. Keys and weights follow the Tensor Core fragment layout, so the kernels can dequantize them directly into MMA operands without creating full intermediate tiles. A block-diagonal Hadamard transform makes INT4 cache quantization less sensitive to outlier channels. On one H100, prefill is up to 1.48 × \times faster than compiled PyTorch FP8 and reaches 1.29 PFLOP/s. For the closest shared operation, gate/up projection followed by SwiGLU, the BF16 path is 1.13 × \times faster than the released CODA kernel at the 8B shape. Our FP8 inference path is 2.02–2.18 × \times faster than the evaluated BF16 CODA path. Across the 8B and 70B shapes at batch 1 to 32, INT4 decode is 1.3–2.4 × \times faster than whichever PyTorch decode block is faster at each point: 2.1–3.3 × \times faster than the compiled, CUDA-graphed BF16 block, and 1.3–6.3 × \times faster than the same block using PyTorch’s INT4 projection kernel, which is built for a single query row and loses to its own BF16 block at batch 32. INT4 decode is also 31–51% faster than our FP8 decode path. For the complete Llama-3.1-8B model, one INT4 decode step takes 2.8 ms at batch one, compared with 8.1 ms for the compiled transformers implementation. On Llama-3.1-8B, decoding every WikiText-2 token through the INT4 weight path increases perplexity from 6.24 to 7.23 with round-to-nearest weights, or to 6.99 with GPTQ weights stored in the same format. The rotated INT4 cache adds another 0.20. The kernel path matches the quantized reference computation to within 0.001 perplexity. 1 Introduction Matrix multiplication dominates Transformer FLOPs, but data movement and other operations also contribute to execution time. A decoder block also performs normalization, residual updates, position encoding, activation functions, precision conversion, and KV-cache updates. These operations perform little arithmetic but often read and write large intermediate tensors. As Tensor Cores become faster, this data movement takes a larger share of the total execution time. CODA Guo et al. (2026) addresses this problem for training by expressing many Transformer operators as GEMM-plus-epilogue programs. An optimized GEMM mainloop produces an output tile. A programmable epilogue then processes the tile while it is still on chip. This allows pairwise operations such as RoPE and SwiGLU, as well as residual updates, scaling, and partial reductions, to run without separate reads and writes to global memory. FuTransformer uses the same GEMM-plus-epilogue principle for autoregressive inference. Inference adds two requirements. First, prefill must manage persistent state. It must write K and V directly to the KV cache, produce low-precision activations for later projections, and support requests of different lengths. Second, decode has too few rows to behave like a large GEMM. At small batch sizes, each layer reads its weights for only a few rows, and attention reads cached K and V values for every query. The decode path must therefore reduce the bytes read and prevent dequantization from delaying the main computation. For prefill, FuTransformer uses persistent FP8 GEMMs with epilogue policies selected at compile time. These policies apply RoPE or SwiGLU, write K and V to the cache, collect RMSNorm statistics, restore scales, and optionally write FP8 output directly. Inference weights are fixed, so the learned RMSNorm gain can be folded into the next projection before quantization. The row-wise normalization factor is then applied in that projection’s epilogue. This removes the normalized activation tensor while preserving the quantized computation. Packed inputs also remove padded projection rows from batches with different request lengths. For decode, FuTransformer uses INT4 weights and an INT4 copy of the KV cache. Hopper has no INT4 Tensor Core MMA, and its FP8 MMA requires large warpgroup shapes that the few query rows in decode cannot fill. The kernel must therefore expand INT4 values before a 16-bit MMA. The main design choice is where to perform this expansion. FuTransformer stores keys and weights in the order required by the MMA fragments. A byte-indexed lookup converts packed cache values into FP16 pairs. A short sequence of logic and packed BF16 operations converts weight nibbles directly in registers. Group scales are applied after accumulation. Before cache quantization, a block-diagonal Hadamard transform spreads large channel values. Matching transforms on the query and attention output preserve the attention computation before quantization. The main contributions are: • Inference-specific GEMM epilogues. Starting from CODA’s GEMM-plus-epilogue formulation, FuTransformer adds direct KV-cache placement, folds the fixed RMSNorm gain into weights, writes FP8 producer output with delayed scaling, and supports packed prefill. • Fragment-aligned INT4 decode. INT4 weights and cache entries are packed in the layout required by the MMA fragments that consume them. Values are dequantized in registers or through a small lookup table. Scales are applied outside the per-element inner loop. • Outlier-aware cache quantization. A block-diagonal Hadamard transform reduces INT4 cache error when keys contain large channel outliers. Before quantization, the transform preserves the exact attention dot product. • A final-result evaluation. We compare full prefill and decode layers with PyTorch. We also compare the complete Llama-3.1-8B model with PyTorch and the closest shared gate/up–SwiGLU stage with CODA. We report performance and numerical error, and label comparisons that use different precisions. Using a trained Llama-3.1-8B checkpoint, we decode every WikiText-2 token through the INT4 path and measure perplexity, per-layer error, and error accumulated across layers. 2 Background and Positioning 2.1 Llama-style inference block Let X ∈ ℝ M × H X\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times H} contain M M token vectors, each with hidden width H H . Let I I denote the feed-forward width, H q H_{q} the number of query heads, H k ​ v H_{kv} the number of KV heads, and D D the head dimension. We evaluate this block: X ^ \displaystyle\widehat{X} = RMSNorm ⁡ ( X , γ 1 ) , \displaystyle=\operatorname{RMSNorm}(X;\gamma_{1}), ( Q , K , V ) \displaystyle(Q,K,V) = X ^ ​ W q ​ k ​ v ⊤ , \displaystyle=\widehat{X}W_{qkv}^{\top}, (1) O \displaystyle O = Attention ⁡ ( RoPE ⁡ ( Q ) , K c , V c ) , \displaystyle=\operatorname{Attention}(\operatorname{RoPE}(Q),K_{c},V_{c}), X 1 \displaystyle X_{1} = X + O ​ W o ⊤ , \displaystyle=X+OW_{o}^{\top}, (2) X ^ 1 \displaystyle\widehat{X}_{1} = RMSNorm ⁡ ( X 1 ; γ 2 ) , \displaystyle=\operatorname{RMSNorm}(X_{1};\gamma_{2}), Z \displaystyle Z = SiLU ⁡ ( X ^ 1 ​ W g ⊤ ) ⊙ ( X ^ 1 ​ W u ⊤ ) , \displaystyle=\operatorname{SiLU}(\widehat{X}_{1}W_{g}^{\top})\odot(\widehat{X}_{1}W_{u}^{\top}), (3) Y \displaystyle Y = X 1 + Z ​ W d ⊤ . \displaystyle=X_{1}+ZW_{d}^{\top}. (4) K c K_{c} and V c V_{c} store the keys and values for earlier tokens and the current token. The block uses causal grouped-query attention (GQA) Ainslie et al. (2023) and RMSNorm Zhang and Sennrich (2019) . The gate and up projections share one GEMM, giving four projection GEMMs and one attention stage in total. During prefill, M = B ​ S M=BS , where B B is the batch size and S S is the sequence length. Each weight tile is reused across many token rows. During single-token decode, M = B M=B . At the small batch sizes studied here, reading the weights accounts for most projection latency. Attention latency grows with context length T T because attention must read the KV cache. 2.2 GEMM-plus-epilogue programs and CODA A high-performance GEMM has two parts. The mainloop loads input tiles and performs matrix multiply-accumulate operations. The epilogue processes and stores each completed output tile. At that point, the output is already in registers or shared memory. The epilogue can therefore perform local operations without first writing an intermediate tensor to HBM. CODA Guo et al. (2026) provides a structured way to use this idea in Transformer training. It keeps the GEMM mainloop fixed and offers five groups of epilogue operations that can be combined: elementwise and pairwise maps; vector loads and stores; tile loads and stores; tile reductions, with partial results combined by a small auxiliary kernel; and stateful transforms. CODA also shows that the row-wise RMSNorm factor can be moved through the following GEMM and applied in its epilogue. Together, these operations cover nearly all non-attention work in the forward and backward passes of a Transformer block. FlashAttention introduced tiled attention designed to reduce data movement, together with online softmax. Later work adapted the execution schedule to newer GPU pipelines and low precision Dao et al. (2022) ; Dao (2024) ; Shah et al. (2024) . FuTransformer ’s prefill attention follows this approach. Its decode design focuses on how low-bit K and V values are stored and expanded into the MMA fragments that use them. 2.3 Low-precision weights and KV caches FP8 E4M3 reduces the data read and written by projections while retaining Tensor Core execution Micikevicius and others (2022) . If A m ​ k ≈ a m ​ A m ​ k q A_{mk}\approx a_{m}A^{q}_{mk} and W n ​ k ≈ b n ​ W n ​ k q W_{nk}\approx b_{n}W^{q}_{nk} , then C ~ m ​ n = a m ​ b n ​ ∑ k A m ​ k q ​ W n ​ k q . \widetilde{C}_{mn}=a_{m}b_{n}\sum_{k}A^{q}_{mk}W^{q}_{nk}. (5) The row and column scales can be applied after accumulation, rather than to every product. Systems such as Transformer Engine use delayed scaling NVIDIA (2026b) : the producer writes FP8 output immediately, using a scale collected during an earlier execution. GPTQ and AWQ made group-scaled INT4 weights practical Frantar et al. (2023) ; Lin and others (2024) . Marlin showed the benefits of packing weights in Tensor Core fragment order and dequantizing them in registers Frantar et al. (2024) . KIVI studied low-bit KV caches Liu et al. (2024) . QuaRot and SAW-INT4 use Hadamard rotations to reduce activation and cache outliers Ashkboos and others (2024) ; Jia et al. (2026) . FuTransformer combines these ideas in a complete Hopper decode block, with layouts designed for its attention and projection fragments. 3 FuTransformer Design 3.1 Overview FuTransformer uses separate prefill and decode paths because they have different bottlenecks. Prefill keeps large GEMMs efficient and reduces data movement between them. Decode reduces the bytes read for weights and the cache, then dequantizes values in the layout required by the MMA operands. The prefill projection kernel uses 128 × 256 × 128 128\times 256\times 128 CTA tiles, a four-stage TMA pipeline, one producer warpgroup, and two consumer warpgroups. Its mainloop uses Hopper FP8 WGMMA and the Tensor Memory Accelerator NVIDIA (2026a) . An epilogue policy selected at compile time controls how each completed fragment is processed and stored. The QKV, output, gate/up, and down projections can therefore perform different inference operations while sharing one optimized GEMM mainloop. The decode path has two kernel families. A register-streaming kernel handles M = 1 M=1 , and a skinny matrix kernel handles 2 ≤ M ≤ 32 2\leq M\leq 32 . Both read packed INT4 weights and expand them directly into MMA fragments for accumulation with BF16 activations. Decode attention reads the INT4 cache copy. For long contexts, it uses split-KV reduction. 3.2 Inference-aware FP8 prefill 3.2.1 Direct KV-cache placement In training, K and V are activations used later in the same pass. In inference, they must be written to persistent cache addresses. A conventional implementation first writes dense K and V tensors, then launches another kernel to scatter them into the cache. FuTransformer writes them to the cache directly from the QKV epilogue. For each output row m m , metadata gives the request and token position p m p_{m} . The epilogue maps each output column to a head and channel in Q, K, or V. It restores the projection scales, applies RoPE to Q and K, writes Q in the layout used by attention, and stores K and V at offset ⁡ ( request ⁡ ( m ) , head , p m , channel ) . \operatorname{offset}(\operatorname{request}(m),\operatorname{head},p_{m},\operatorname{channel}). (6) Each cache element has one writer, and elements outside the valid range are masked. This removes the dense K/V intermediate tensors and the separate cache-scatter pass. 3.2.2 Folding the frozen RMSNorm gain The block applies RMSNorm before the QKV and gate/up projections. Define q m = ∑ h x m ​ h 2 , ρ m = ( q m / H + ϵ ) − 1 / 2 . q_{m}=\sum_{h}x_{mh}^{2},\qquad\rho_{m}=\left(q_{m}/H+\epsilon\right)^{-1/2}. (7) For projection weight row W n W_{n} and learned gain γ \gamma , the output is C m ​ n \displaystyle C_{mn} = ∑ h x m ​ h ​ ρ m ​ γ h ​ W n ​ h = ρ m ​ ∑ h x m ​ h ​ W n ​ h ′ , \displaystyle=\sum_{h}x_{mh}\rho_{m}\gamma_{h}W_{nh}=\rho_{m}\sum_{h}x_{mh}W^{\prime}_{nh}, W n ​ h ′ \displaystyle W^{\prime}_{nh} = γ h ​ W n ​ h . \displaystyle=\gamma_{h}W_{nh}. (8) CODA moves the row factor ρ m \rho_{m} through the next GEMM and applies it in that GEMM’s epilogue. During inference, γ \gamma and W W are fixed. FuTransformer therefore folds γ \gamma into W W once, before quantizing and repacking the weights. The GEMM then reads the raw activation X X and the preprocessed weight W ′ W^{\prime} . With FP8 operands, the output is C ~ m ​ n = ρ m ​ a m ​ b n ​ ∑ h X m ​ h q ​ ( W ′ ) n ​ h q . \widetilde{C}_{mn}=\rho_{m}a_{m}b_{n}\sum_{h}X^{q}_{mh}(W^{\prime})^{q}_{nh}. (9) The epilogue that produces the residual stream also computes partial sums of squares. A small reduction combines the results from all output tiles to obtain q m q_{m} . The next projection uses ρ m \rho_{m} , so no normalized activation tensor needs to be written to HBM. 3.2.3 Delayed FP8 emission The down projection reads the SwiGLU output Z Z . If the gate/up epilogue writes this output in BF16, a separate quantization kernel must read it and write an FP8 copy. For M M rows and feed-forward width I I , the two approaches move ℬ separate = 5 ​ M ​ I , ℬ producer = M ​ I , \mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{separate}}=5MI,\qquad\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{producer}}=MI, (10) bytes, respectively. The separate path writes BF16, reads it again, and writes FP8. The producer path writes FP8 only once. FuTransformer uses delayed per-tensor scaling. Invocation t t quantizes its output with the maximum collected during invocation t − 1 t-1 . At the same time, the epilogue computes the current maximum magnitude for invocation t + 1 t+1 . It can therefore process and store each fragment immediately. The kernel does not need to keep a full output row in memory on chip while waiting for a global maximum. The scale state has three requirements. The first invocation must have a valid initial scale. A scale must also be defined for all-zero tensors. Concurrent request groups must keep separate scale states unless they are intentionally run together. Production use also needs saturation counters, because a sudden change in value range can make the previous scale unsuitable. 3.2.4 Packed prefill For requests with lengths S 1 , … , S B S_{1},\ldots,S_{B} , padded execution processes B ​ max b ​ S b B\max_{b}S_{b} rows. Packed execution processes only M packed = ∑ b = 1 B S b . M_{\mathrm{packed}}=\sum_{b=1}^{B}S_{b}. (11) A prefix-sum array maps each packed row to its request and token position. This mapping also defines attention boundaries and KV-cache locations. FuTransformer compiles separate kernels for padded and packed inputs, so the padded path does not need runtime layout checks. 3.3 Fragment-aligned INT4 decode 3.3.1 Why decode needs a different path Let P P be the number of projection-weight elements in one layer. Excluding small metadata fields, the minimum number of bytes read during decode is ℬ decode = P ​ w + 2 ​ B ​ T ​ H k ​ v ​ D ​ k , \mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{decode}}=Pw+2BTH_{kv}Dk, (12) Here, w w is the number of bytes per weight, and k k is the number of bytes per cached K or V element. For the 8B shape at batch one, the projection weights contain 218.1 million elements. These weights occupy 436 MB in BF16, 218 MB in E4M3, or 109 MB in INT4. Reducing w w and k k therefore directly reduces the data that must be read and can lower latency. On H100, the small- M M decode kernels cannot use an INT4 MMA that directly reads these packed values. They also have too few rows for the large FP8 WGMMA shapes used in prefill. FuTransformer therefore expands low-bit values into 16-bit MMA operands. Its layouts allow this expansion to happen while building the fragments, without a separate dequantization stage. 3.3.2 INT4 KV-cache mirror FuTransformer keeps the BF16 KV cache as the main copy for prefill and compatibility, and maintains an INT4 copy for decode. Each byte stores two signed 4-bit values. Each token and KV head has one FP32 scale, calculated as amax / 7 \operatorname{amax}/7 . Scaling is performed outside the elementwise loop. For K, the scale is applied to the completed query–key dot product. For V, it is applied to the attention probability before the probability–value MMA. The kernel therefore avoids scaling each unpacked element separately. A shared-memory table with 256 entries maps each packed byte to two FP16 values. One lookup expands both nibbles into the pair format needed by an MMA fragment. The table does not depend on the token scale, because scales are applied after accumulation. Keys follow the byte order required by the B operand of mma.sync.m16n8k16 . Each lane reads a contiguous segment the size of its fragment and uses byte-indexed lookups to fill the operand registers directly. This avoids creating a dequantized K tile and moving it through shared memory. V stays in natural channel order because the probability–value MMA groups values differently. It is transposed through shared memory before use. The attention CTA quantizes the new cache row that it will use in the current decode step. The asynchronous-copy pipeline loads cache scales together with their K/V tile. This keeps cache updates and scale loads outside the serial inner attention loop. 3.3.3 Hadamard transform for cache outliers Uniform INT4 quantization can lose accuracy when a few channels have large values. Following QuaRot and SAW-INT4 Ashkboos and others (2024) ; Jia et al. (2026) , FuTransformer applies a normalized block-diagonal Hadamard matrix H H before writing each cache row. The query uses the same transform: ( H ​ q ) ⊤ ​ ( H ​ k ) = q ⊤ ​ H ⊤ ​ H ​ k = q ⊤ ​ k . (Hq)^{\top}(Hk)=q^{\top}H^{\top}Hk=q^{\top}k. (13) The attention output is transformed back once per query row. The transform uses a Walsh–Hadamard butterfly implemented with registers and warp shuffles. Each cache row is rotated once when it is written. The query and output are each rotated once per decode step. The attention loop therefore performs the same work per cached token, and the added rotation cost does not grow with context length. By default, each block covers the full head dimension, but narrower blocks can also be used. 3.3.4 INT4 projection weights Weights are quantized offline with one symmetric scale for each output channel and each group of 128 input elements. The nibbles follow the order required by the B fragments of the decode MMA, so each warp can load a contiguous weight segment for its output tile. The format defines where each nibble is stored, not how its value is chosen. Values can come from the library’s round-to-nearest quantizer or a calibrated method such as GPTQ. Both quantization grids are packed into the same layout offline. Weights are dequantized in registers. Each nibble is inserted into the mantissa bits of the BF16 value 128.0. A logic operation produces packed BF16 values of the form ( 128 + n , 128 + m ) (128+n,128+m) . One packed BF16 fused multiply-add then subtracts 136. This removes the base value 128 and the offset of 8 used to convert an unsigned nibble to a signed value. Each group is accumulated separately. Its group scale is applied before the result is added to the running FP32 accumulator. The kernel never creates a full BF16 weight tile. For M = 1 M=1 , each warp reads the weights for one output tile and a quarter of the reduction dimension. The four warps in a CTA combine their partial sums through shared memory. For 2 ≤ M ≤ 32 2\leq M\leq 32 , a skinny kernel loads activation tiles, packed weights, and scales through a multi-stage asynchronous-copy pipeline. It uses split-K across CTAs when additional CTAs are needed to keep the GPU occupied. 4 Evaluation 4.1 Experimental setup We run the experiments on one NVIDIA H100 80GB SXM5 GPU with CUDA 13.0 and PyTorch 2.14.1+cu130. For prefill and CODA measurements, the SM clock is fixed at 1980 MHz. Decode measurements use default clocks. We interleave the compared implementations within the same run so that they experience similar thermal conditions. Unless stated otherwise, compiled PyTorch and FuTransformer both use CUDA graphs. Prefill results are the median of four to eight timing invocations after warm-up. For CODA, we alternate the two binaries over three rounds. For decode, all PyTorch and FuTransformer candidates run in one process over three interleaved rounds. Both comparisons report median CUDA event time over repeated launches. Each table is a separate interleaved run, so the same configuration can differ by up to 2% between tables; each comparison is made within one table. The per-layer tests use synthetic inputs and weights, quantized with the library’s round-to-nearest quantizer. The whole-model tests in Section 4.5 use the trained checkpoint and the GPTQ-packed weights described in Section 4.8 . The quantizer changes the nibble values but not their number or storage positions, so it does not change latency. The two quantizers give the same timing within run-to-run variation. The labels 1B, 8B, 70B, and 405B refer to layer shapes. They do not imply that a complete model of that size runs on one GPU. Table 1: Llama-style layer shapes evaluated in this paper. Across the 8B and 70B shapes at batch 1 to 32, INT4 decode is 1.3–2.4 × \times faster than whichever PyTorch decode block is faster at each point: 2.1–3.3 × \times faster than the compiled, CUDA-graphed BF16 block, and 1.3–6.3 × \times faster than the same block using PyTorch’s INT4 projection kernel, which is built for a single query row and loses to its own BF16 block at batch 32. INT4 decode is also 31–51% faster than our FP8 decode path. For the complete Llama-3.1-8B model, one INT4 decode step takes 2.8 ms at batch one, compared with 8.1 ms for the compiled transformers implementation. On Llama-3.1-8B, decoding every WikiText-2 token through the INT4 weight path increases perplexity from 6.24 to 7.23 with round-to-nearest weights, or to 6.99 with GPTQ weights stored in the same format. The rotated INT4 cache adds another 0.20. The kernel path matches the quantized reference computation to within 0.001 perplexity. 1 Introduction Matrix multiplication dominates Transformer FLOPs, but data movement and other operations also contribute to execution time. A decoder block also performs normalization, residual updates, position encoding, activation functions, precision conversion, and KV-cache updates. These operations perform little arithmetic but often read and write large intermediate tensors. As Tensor Cores become faster, this data movement takes a larger share of the total execution time. CODA Guo et al. (2026) addresses this problem for training by expressing many Transformer operators as GEMM-plus-epilogue programs. An optimized GEMM mainloop produces an output tile. A programmable epilogue then processes the tile while it is still on chip. This allows pairwise operations such as RoPE and SwiGLU, as well as residual updates, scaling, and partial reductions, to run without separate reads and writes to global memory. FuTransformer uses the same GEMM-plus-epilogue principle for autoregressive inference. Inference adds two requirements. First, prefill must manage persistent state. It must write K and V directly to the KV cache, produce low-precision activations for later projections, and support requests of different lengths. Second, decode has too few rows to behave like a large GEMM. At small batch sizes, each layer reads its weights for only a few rows, and attention reads cached K and V values for every query. The decode path must therefore reduce the bytes read and prevent dequantization from delaying the main computation. For prefill, FuTransformer uses persistent FP8 GEMMs with epilogue policies selected at compile time. These policies apply RoPE or SwiGLU, write K and V to the cache, collect RMSNorm statistics, restore scales, and optionally write FP8 output directly. Inference weights are fixed, so the learned RMSNorm gain can be folded into the next projection before quantization. The row-wise normalization factor is then applied in that projection’s epilogue. This removes the normalized activation tensor while preserving the quantized computation. Packed inputs also remove padded projection rows from batches with different request lengths. For decode, FuTransformer uses INT4 weights and an INT4 copy of the KV cache. Hopper has no INT4 Tensor Core MMA, and its FP8 MMA requires large warpgroup shapes that the few query rows in decode cannot fill. The kernel must therefore expand INT4 values before a 16-bit MMA. The main design choice is where to perform this expansion. FuTransformer stores keys and weights in the order required by the MMA fragments. A byte-indexed lookup converts packed cache values into FP16 pairs. A short sequence of logic and packed BF16 operations converts weight nibbles directly in registers. Group scales are applied after accumulation. Before cache quantization, a block-diagonal Hadamard transform spreads large channel values. Matching transforms on the query and attention output preserve the attention computation before quantization. The main contributions are: • Inference-specific GEMM epilogues. Starting from CODA’s GEMM-plus-epilogue formulation, FuTransformer adds direct KV-cache placement, folds the fixed RMSNorm gain into weights, writes FP8 producer output with delayed scaling, and supports packed prefill. • Fragment-aligned INT4 decode. INT4 weights and cache entries are packed in the layout required by the MMA fragments that consume them. Values are dequantized in registers or through a small lookup table. Scales are applied outside the per-element inner loop. • Outlier-aware cache quantization. A block-diagonal Hadamard transform reduces INT4 cache error when keys contain large channel outliers. Before quantization, the transform preserves the exact attention dot product. • A final-result evaluation. We compare full prefill and decode layers with PyTorch. We also compare the complete Llama-3.1-8B model with PyTorch and the closest shared gate/up–SwiGLU stage with CODA. We report performance and numerical error, and label comparisons that use different precisions.
